papers.title: Price co-movement and price information diverge across Nordic electricity zones after the energy crisis
papers.summary: After the 2021-2022 energy crisis, day-ahead prices in Nordic bidding zones no longer move together. We ask whether this divergence also changes the information carried by prices. The answer matters for integrating variable renewable energy (VRE), because it can help identify where wind and solar forecasts are worth producing, publishing, and using. We measured the co-movement of each Norwegian and Swedish zone with Germany-Luxembourg (DE-LU) in 2018-2025. We then used a single model, selected on 2024 data, to forecast 2025 prices at 11:00 on the previous day and tested which inputs improved accuracy in each zone. The zones moved alike until 2019, but co-movement diverged in Sweden in 2020 and in Norway in 2021, and the split has persisted. In 2024, four southern zones co-moved strongly with DE-LU (intraday correlations of 0.54-0.71), while four northern zones co-moved weakly (0.25-0.30). Yet price information did not follow this split. Previous-day neighbouring prices reduced mean absolute error by at most 2.2% in any zone, equally in coupled and isolated zones. Removing the transmission system operators' wind and solar forecasts increased mean absolute error by at most 6% in Norway, 8-16% in Sweden, and 31% in DE-LU, and the ordering held in 2024. Within Norway, the value of these forecasts showed no detectable dependence on reservoir filling. The divergence in co-movement was therefore not matched by a divergence in price information, which differed mainly between national generation systems. Thus, a zone's coupling to the continent does not indicate the value of VRE forecasts there.

authors.name: My Thi Diem Phan, Tuyen Trung Truong, Hoai Phuong Ha, Dat Thanh Nguyen

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Training Data Generation Strategies for Machine Learning-Based Molecular and Materials Property Prediction
papers.summary: Machine-learning (ML) models for molecular and materials property prediction are often trained on large datasets curated through arbitrary or generic sampling strategies. Such approaches can lead to the over- or under-representation of regions of chemical and materials space that are most relevant to the prediction task. An important challenge is therefore how to efficiently curate training data to maximize predictive performance while minimising the number of labelled examples required. Here, we systematically compare training data acquisition strategies for molecular and materials property prediction, ranging from random sampling to various active learning approaches. We evaluate their performance across different model classes, representations, datasets, and target properties. Our results show that the effectiveness of data acquisition strategies depend strongly on the interplay between the model, dataset, and prediction task, although uncertainty-based sampling generally outperforms alternative strategies. Based on these findings, we derive guidelines for selecting data acquisition strategies under a given labelling budget.

authors.name: Minh Nghia Nguyen, Beate Paulus, Akhil S. Nair

papers.title: Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition: Information, Uncertainty, and Conditional Regime Inference
papers.summary: When do mode energies preserve regime information as measurement quality changes? Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition (sKMD) fits joint regime laws on signed KMD mode coordinates and transfers the reference mode posterior to regime probabilities and conditional reconstructions. For centered Gaussian regimes with independently varying known noise variances, fixed coordinate energies retain the full regime posterior precisely when all classes share their cross-covariances and class variances can differ only at isolated vertices of the covariance graph. We extend the characterization to nonzero means and show that freely varying correlated noise forces a fixed linear log-odds decoder to retain the full quadratic feature span even for two distinct centered regimes. At fixed quality, a three-regime example has no sufficient two-energy basis. Its smallest Bayes log-loss gap over bases of condition number at most $\kappa$ has sharp order $\kappa^{-1}$. Exact Bayes energy posteriors supply numerical gap estimates for specified bases. Additional bounds relate feature compression, independently learned mode spans and sensor-noise error to log loss. Two controlled experiments with 64 independent panels each show that signed information can improve prediction over energy summaries, while integration gives small gains over strong signed controls and depends on how the competing point rule is calibrated and how accurately observation noise is measured.

authors.name: Boumediene Hamzi, Houman Owhadi

papers.title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models
papers.summary: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.

authors.name: Yik Siu Chan, Jing Huang, Yanai Elazar, Atticus Geiger

papers.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
papers.summary: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.

authors.name: Shourik Banerjee, Ethan Mendes, Mohit Raghavendra, Wei Xu, Alan Ritter

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory
papers.summary: A large body of work in quantum machine learning has centered on characterizing the expressivity and performance of quantum models. In contrast, little attention has been paid to the reliability of predictions beyond average performance measures such as accuracy. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware quantum classification framework based on Dempster-Shafer theory. This theory allows to express uncertainty through weights assigned not only to individual classification labels but to sets of labels. We introduce a training strategy that enables parameterized quantum circuits to learn such assignments directly from data. This provides an efficient way to prepare the corresponding quantum states and enables the application of different post-processing strategies. In particular, it offers a practical setting for quantum Dempster-Shafer fusion procedures with polynomial resource requirements, even when the corresponding mass functions are defined over exponentially many subsets. Overall, our work represents a step toward enabling quantum models to express uncertainty about their predictions, thereby extending the evaluation of quantum models beyond predictive performance alone.

authors.name: Marie Kempkes, Jakob Spiegelberg, Evert van Nieuwenburg, Vedran Dunjko

papers.title: An Integrated Architecture for Data-Efficient Real-Time Neural Imitation of Nonlinear Time-Optimal Model Predictive Control
papers.summary: Nonlinear time-optimal model predictive control (TOMPC) enables highly performant control of constrained systems, but its computational cost prohibits real-time use on fast dynamical systems. Neural network imitation of the TOMPC control law can reduce online computational costs, yet existing work mostly targets quadratic cost formulations in simulation and addresses the challenges of neural controllers in isolation. This work imitates a long-horizon nonconvex TOMPC with hard terminal constraints, whose high computational cost limits training-data generation. We present (i) \emph{self-informed sampling (SIFS)}, a data-efficient expert-sampling strategy that uses a learned time-to-go to query the expert only where the policy deviates from time-optimal behavior, (ii) a complete training and control architecture that jointly addresses dataset correlation, suboptimal expert labels, covariate shift, constraint satisfaction and model mismatch, and (iii) real-world validation on a Furuta pendulum. SIFS matches standard dataset aggregation performance in roughly one-third of the training time and with less than half the training data. The resulting controller matches the region of attraction of the expert TOMPC while raising the control frequency from 1.4~Hz to 1~kHz. On hardware, the controller swings up and stabilizes the pendulum along trajectories closely matching the expert TOMPC solution.

authors.name: Maarten De Baecke, Flavia Sofia Acerbo, Andrea Giusti, Wilm Decr\'e

papers.title: Random Exploration is Random
papers.summary: Decision making often requires balancing exploitation of familiar options with exploration of uncertain alternatives. One strategy for exploration is random exploration, in which choices become more variable and less tied to the option that currently appears best. However, it remains unclear whether this variability reflects genuine stochasticity or instead a deterministic structure that traditional cognitive models fail to capture. We examined this question using the Horizon Task in an aggregated dataset of 1,392 participants completing over 1,270,695 trials. In this task, exploration becomes more valuable when participants have more future choices, and choice variability increases under longer horizons. We tested whether more expressive neural network models could recover deterministic structure from this additional variability. Although neural networks provided better overall fits to behavior than the traditional model, long-horizon choices remained consistently less predictable than short-horizon choices. These findings show that limited model expressiveness cannot fully account for the increased variability associated with random exploration, suggesting random exploration truly is substantially random.

authors.name: Yingkang Luo, Hua-Dong Xiong, Hanbo Xie, Caroline Phelps, Madeline Harms, Ryan Smith, James Waltz, Robert Wilson

papers.title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity
papers.summary: Watermark detectors decide whether one document came from a watermarked language model. Auditors often need a different number: the share of a corpus that did. We study this share for Gumbel-max and green-list (KGW) watermarks when every document may have been edited by an unknown amount. Without restrictions on the edits, the upper end of the identified set is 1. Combining a known least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, we derive a power envelope indexed by three budgets: a retention floor, an entropy budget, and a budget for in-place substitutions, which for Gumbel-max make edited positions look less watermarked than human text. The envelope gives an identified set that is sharp for the alternatives it dominates, finite-sample bounds on the realized share of a fixed corpus with either the exact null or a null calibrated on an independent human sample, and confidence sequences for streams. In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover, and the threshold that maximizes the gap between envelope and null is generally as tight as twelve thresholds. On text from OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B, 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys show no robust departure from the exact null, and all bounds covered in resampling trials from finite pools of documents with random edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14,0.38]. These results are fragile in two ways we make precise. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet at 2000 documents the bounds still covered in these trials. A simulated null error of 0.01, comparable to the largest deviation we observed at our thresholds, is likewise harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000; a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage there, but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.

authors.name: Kuancheng Ye

papers.title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
papers.summary: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

authors.name: Yihan Xia, Wenxin Xu, Taotao Wang

papers.title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
papers.summary: Structured Electronic Health Records (EHR) models typically treat each clinical concept as a dataset-specific token, discarding the natural-language semantics associated with the event. As a result, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence, without directly exploiting any prior semantic knowledge. We investigate how pretrained causal language models can be adapted for longitudinal EHR prediction by developing tEHR. Here, we represent events with their natural language description and use this text stream to apply EHR-adaptive continued pretraining, followed by task-specific discriminative fine-tuning using LoRA, utilising the LLM as a longitudinal patient-encoder. We evaluate this approach across four prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset and pancreatic cancer prediction on the CPRD dataset at 1 to 12 month horizons, with tEHR using the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone achieving the strongest overall performance. Ablations show that performance declines when clinical descriptions are removed or misaligned, when numerical values are omitted, and when either stage of adaptation is removed, while explicit elapsed-time descriptions provide little additional benefit. Analysis of the learned patient representations further reveals clinically coherent structure associated with distinct patterns of disease risk and clinical history.

authors.name: Ashvin Gupta, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo

papers.title: An Invariant Neural-Network Eddy-Viscosity Closure with Iterative Solver Coupling for Molten Salt Fast Reactor Thermal-Hydraulics
papers.summary: System thermal-hydraulics codes such as the System Analysis Module (SAM) close turbulence on coarse meshes with algebraic zero-equation mixing-length models. These models cannot represent the non-equilibrium turbulence, flow separation, and large-scale recirculation of open-cavity advanced reactors. We develop an invariant neural-network eddy-viscosity closure for SAM and apply it to the Molten Salt Fast Reactor (MSFR). The closure predicts the turbulent kinetic energy and timescale of each element from the flow and geometry of its neighbors, without solving turbulence transport equations. The resulting non-negative eddy viscosity enters the implicit diffusive operator, which keeps the momentum equations well conditioned. We prove that the closure is exactly invariant to translation, Galilean boost, rotation, reflection, and neighbor ordering. A network trained on high-order Nek5000 fields sees a different feature distribution on the coarse SAM mesh. We remove this covariate shift by iteratively retraining the network on SAM flow states against fixed Nek5000 targets. For a held-out steady state, the coupled closure reproduces the single recirculation cell and eddy-viscosity plume of the Nek5000 reference. In a 120 s pump-coastdown transient, it halves the velocity error of the mixing-length model, from 37.6% to 17.7%, and matches the Nek5000 eddy viscosity with a time-averaged relative error of 12%. The remaining velocity error comes from the coarse mesh. The coupled transient takes about 0.2 core-hours, compared with about 330 core-hours for Nek5000. The results show that the closure can recover two-equation RANS turbulence behavior in a coarse-mesh system code at a small fraction of the CFD cost.

authors.name: Zaid Abulawi (Department of Nuclear Engineering, Texas A&M University), William Oliveira (Department of Energy, Nuclear Engineering Division, Politecnico di Milano), Akzhol Almukhametov (Department of Nuclear Engineering, Texas A&M University), Jun Fang (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division, Argonne National Laboratory), Ling Zou (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division, Argonne National Laboratory), Rui Hu (Nuclear Science and Engineering Division, Argonne National Laboratory), Stefano Lorenzi (Department of Energy, Nuclear Engineering Division, Politecnico di Milano), Yang Liu (Department of Nuclear Engineering, Texas A&M University)

papers.title: Joint Null-Space Projection for Data-Free Model Merging
papers.summary: Merging independently fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model requires no data, no labels, and no gradient steps. In practice the task vectors of different tasks interfere, and the standard remedies--averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election--operate entry by entry, ignoring that each delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon. We recast merging as a subspace interference problem. For every two-dimensional weight tensor we take the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta--the input directions along which that task moves the representation most--and remove from each task vector the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces. The resulting Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set. On eight CLIP image-classification tasks JNSP merges ViT-B/16 experts to 89.45% average accuracy without using a single image, 11.88 points above the strongest parameter-wise training-free baseline (TIES-Merging, 77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic, and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). The gain holds across three backbones on the independently trained TALL release (+10.8, +12.6, +9.1 over TIES for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) and replicates there at 89.20%; controls confirm the source--a single shared subspace instead of per-task ones loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the same projection underperforms plain task arithmetic, which we report rather than hide. Code is available at https://github.com.

authors.name: Tian Xia

papers.title: STeP-C: Real-Time Neural Compression for Distributed Fiber-Optic Sensing at Scale
papers.summary: Distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) technologies such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) generate continuous, high-resolution spatio-temporal data at rates exceeding hundreds of megabytes per second, creating severe challenges for real-time storage and transmission. While neural compression methods can achieve strong rate-distortion performance on sensing data, prior approaches either require per-segment retraining incompatible with streaming, or have only been validated offline. None have been demonstrated end-to-end on a continuously streaming DAS acquisition system at scale. We present STeP-C (Spatio-Temporal Predictive Compression), a neural compression framework that decouples spatial encoding, temporal prediction, and entropy-optimized residual coding, trained end-to-end with a rate-distortion objective motivated by conditional entropy reduction. Critically, we identify entropy coding as the dominant bottleneck for streaming deployment. We address it through GPU-side symbol computation, cached probability tables, and parallel GIL-free arithmetic coding, together with FP16 inference and batched entropy coding, enabling a full real-time pipeline built around a GPU ring buffer. We validate this pipeline on a live DAS testbed, achieving a 98.85% file size reduction at 31.04 dB full-band PSNR and an average throughput of 535 MB/s, exceeding the 324 MB/s requirement for 1 kHz, 81 km DAS streams. We further show that STeP-C substantially outperforms conventional codecs at practical streaming bitrates, can be applied to unseen channel ranges within the same acquisition system without retraining, and largely maintains downstream detector consistency, with 96.62% high-confidence class agreement and 100% Jaccard similarity on detected event types.

authors.name: Tingfeng Li, Ming-Fang Huang, Shaobo Han, Yue Tian

papers.title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing
papers.summary: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

authors.name: Umar Ahmed, Maxim Dunaev, Mohammad Nour Al Awad, Sergey Ivanov, Ivan Khodnenko

papers.title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Sparse Convolution
papers.summary: Deep neural networks for image processing are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge devices such as drones, medical systems, and smartphones, where limited computational resources and memory bandwidth pose significant challenges for efficient inference. Pruning during training often produces highly sparse convolutional kernels, offering the potential to significantly reduce computation and memory requirements. However, exploiting this sparsity efficiently at runtime remains challenging due to irregular memory access patterns and workload imbalance across processing elements. In this work, we investigate the standard convolution with sparse weights and analyze its performance characteristics through roofline analysis, showing that a 3 x 3 sparse convolution achieves an arithmetic intensity of approximately 10 FLOP/byte compared to roughly 96 FLOP/byte for its dense counterpart. We propose techniques for an efficient sparse convolution at high sparsities. Preliminary results demonstrate that our approach achieves upto 1.65x speedup as compared to dense convolution on NVIDIA A100 and upto 1.52x on NVIDIA Jetson Nano (Tegra X1) , motivating further exploration of direct convolution as a practical path to efficient sparse inference on modern accelerators/edge devices.

authors.name: Keshvi Tuteja, Yu-Hsiang Tsai, Gregor Olenik, Markus G\"otz, Achim Streit, Hartwig Anzt, Charlotte Debus

papers.title: Combinatorial Bernoulli Factories with Polynomially Many Coins
papers.summary: We provide an efficient implementation of combinatorial Bernoulli factories. Such a factory turns coins of unknown biases $x$ into a random vertex of a polytope $P$ whose mean is exactly $x$. For every affine slice of the cube (the class of polytopes that admit a factory), we give a single algorithm whose expected number of coin flips and running time at every interior $x$ are polynomial in the dimension and in $1/{\delta_*}$, where ${\delta_*}=\min_i\{x_i,1-x_i\}$ is never supplied to the algorithm. For perfect matchings this gives $O(n^{8}{\delta_*}^{-2}\log(n/{\delta_*}))$ flips, while the factory of Niazadeh, Paes Leme, and Schneider [STOC 2021] spends at least $n^{2n-1}$ flips in expectation at the uniform doubly stochastic matrix. For other polytopes, our method rounds exactly given a point deep inside $P$ and the promise that $x$ is far from the boundary of $P$.

authors.name: Renato Paes Leme, Rad Niazadeh

papers.title: Data Archive for 2D and 3D Electrical Impedance Tomography with moderate conductivity contrast phantoms
papers.summary: This document describes open Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) measurement data that were collected from biomedical imaging inspired phantoms with moderate conductivity contrasts. The data were collected with the KIT4 and KIT5 EIT measurement devices at the University of Eastern Finland, and are intended for EIT image reconstruction algorithm development and testing. The data from thoracic imaging inspired cylindrical and chest-shaped phantoms are suitable for 2D algorithms, and the data from an intracerebral hemorrhage imaging inspired head-shaped phantom with resistive skull are suitable for 3D algorithms. In addition to the measurement data, computational meshes and example reconstruction codes are provided and sample reconstructions included.

authors.name: S. J. Hamilton, A. Hauptmann, A. H\"anninen, V. Kolehmainen, J. Niskanen, T. Savolainen, J. Toivanen

papers.title: Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering
papers.summary: Graph-based collaborative filtering learns user and item representations by propagating embeddings over a user--item interaction graph. We investigate a modular, sheaf-inspired scoring extension placed on top of a three-layer LightGCN backbone. The motivation comes from cellular sheaves, where local vector spaces are related by linear restriction maps; here, this idea motivates structured, pair-dependent transformations of user and item embeddings rather than a change to graph propagation. We compare the identity inner-product scorer, diagonal, rank-one low-rank, and full matrix residual scorers, and a parameter-matched residual MLP baseline (\texttt{mlp\_full}) on Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018. We report ranking quality and catalog coverage at cutoffs 10 and 20. The selected structured variants show modest, dataset-dependent changes in ranking quality and sometimes substantial changes in coverage. Our method is inspired by sheaf geometry but does not construct a cellular sheaf or implement sheaf-Laplacian diffusion; the experiments therefore do not establish a causal benefit from sheaf geometry itself.

authors.name: Ksenia Belkovskaya, Timur Lidzhiev, Maria Stebliy, Alexander Tarakanov

papers.title: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
papers.summary: We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$. Prior works exhaustively search over a $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the regressors, using conditional moments of the response to test candidates. In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.

authors.name: Felix Zhou

papers.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

authors.name: Tiago de Souza Farias, Caio Moraes Porto, Matheus da Silva Fonseca, Nicolas Armando Cabrera Carpi, Anderson de Araujo Oliveira, Celso Jorge Villas-Boas

papers.title: FLEX-LBP: Learning Local Binary Patterns with Exact Binary Inference for Texture Classification
papers.summary: Local Binary Patterns (LBP) remain among the most widely used texture descriptors, from industrial inspection to medical imaging. Yet their radius, sampling angles, color transform and thresholds are fixed by hand for each dataset. We present FLEX-LBP, which learns these parameters by backpropagation while every forward pass computes exact binary codes and hard histogram counts. A straight-through estimator acts only in the backward pass, so the deployed descriptor is an interpretable hard-binary LBP with 90 learnable parameters and unchanged inference cost. In a controlled ablation on six color texture benchmarks, the component worth learning is dataset-dependent. One configuration, applied unchanged everywhere, learns the geometry and thresholds with the color transform frozen. It improves the nearest-neighbor accuracy of the identical fixed descriptor by 3.55 points on average over five seeds, significantly on five of six benchmarks and never significantly worse. With a linear discriminant readout, it gains 0.9 points; the fully learned descriptor gains 2.7 and has the highest mean. FLEX-LBP is more accurate than five classical LBP-family descriptors, PCANet and a neural LBP on five of six benchmarks. Its mean nearest-neighbor accuracy exceeds that of frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 features (23.5 million parameters). On the Kather colorectal cancer histology benchmark, the fully learned descriptor reaches 93.8%, significantly above the best classical descriptor (Completed LBP, 92.8%). The learned radii adapt in directions that recur across seeds. Noise drowns single-pixel comparisons and illuminant change flips inter-channel ones; median sampling or gray-world normalization restores 96-97%. The code is available as a drop-in PyTorch layer at https://github.com/medalimoussa/FLEX-LBP.

authors.name: Mohamed Alimoussa, Amal El Kaid

papers.title: Quantifying structural stability of transparent models for general insurance pricing
papers.summary: The short duration of general insurance contracts leads to rapid distributional shifts in the data, warranting regular model updates. This process may yield a post-update model that differs considerably from the pre-update model in both predictions and structure. Structural stability is upstream of predictive stability, yet existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees. Thus, we first introduce the notion of functional transparency, characterising models with a prediction function that can be expressed as a sum of univariate functions for main effects and bivariate functions for pairwise interactions. Then, we propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance, a metric to quantify the structural stability of functionally transparent models, which are particularly relevant in actuarial science. Using three public auto insurance datasets, we present a benchmark study to demonstrate the usefulness of our metric in identifying a stable and accurate transparent model. Generalised linear models with centred numerical covariates are stable, and explainable boosting machines (EBMs) offer a compromise between stability and performance. We also find that stabilisation strategies, such as sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters, can substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost models, with negligible impact on performance.

authors.name: F\'elix C\^ot\'e, Marie-Pier C\^ot\'e

papers.title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
papers.summary: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

authors.name: Jie Wang, Tong Zhu, JiaHao Kuang, Zhe Xu, Yunkai Chai, Dehong Zheng, Yu Cheng, Tao Ji, ZhouHan Lin, Qi Zhang, Bowen Zhou

papers.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
papers.summary: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

authors.name: Ellis Brown, Chris Hoang, Shengyi Qian, Shang-Wen Li, Mike Lewis, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Luke Zettlemoyer, Lucas Beyer, Mengye Ren, Jakob Verbeek, Saining Xie, Hu Xu

papers.title: Improved Streaming Algorithm for Balanced Hypergraph Partitioning
papers.summary: Balanced hypergraph partitioning is an essential task for massive hypergraph analysis in distributed computing. Existing methods usually use the entire hypergraph to obtain structural information before the assignment process. However, many applications require online partitioning, motivating the development of streaming algorithms. In the streaming order, vertices are assigned in real time and their ownership does not change. Therefore, partitioning the streamed vertices under the balance constraint is challenging. In this paper, we propose a method for balanced hypergraph partitioning in the streaming mode. By defining a modularity function under the Erdos-Renyi random hypergraph model, we build the Erdos-Renyi Hypergraph Modularity Greedy. We approximate the hypergraph as a uniform hypergraph and optimize the modularity function with lower computational complexity. Compared with other modularity functions, our modularity function is more suitable for streaming algorithms. Finally, we design a data structure to reduce the execution time for finding the block with minimum capacity. Overall, our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance when evaluated with the cut-net metric.

authors.name: Zhicheng Guo

papers.title: CAMRI Loss: Improving the Recall of a Specific Class without Sacrificing Accuracy
papers.summary: In real-world applications of multiclass classification models, misclassification in an important class (e.g., stop sign) can be significantly more harmful than in other classes (e.g., no parking). Thus, it is crucial to improve the recall of an important class while maintaining overall accuracy. For this problem, we found that improving the separation of important classes relative to other classes in the feature space is effective. Existing methods that give a class-sensitive penalty for cross-entropy loss do not improve the separation. Moreover, the methods designed to improve separations between all classes are unsuitable for our purpose because they do not consider the important classes. To achieve the separation, we propose a loss function that explicitly gives loss for the feature space, called class-sensitive additive angular margin (CAMRI) loss. CAMRI loss is expected to reduce the variance of an important class due to the addition of a penalty to the angle between the important class features and the corresponding weight vectors in the feature space. In addition, concentrating the penalty on only the important class hardly sacrifices separating the other classes. Experiments on CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and AwA2 showed that CAMRI loss could improve the recall of a specific class without sacrificing accuracy. In particular, compared with GTSRB's second-worst class recall when trained with cross-entropy loss, CAMRI loss improved recall by 9%.

authors.name: Daiki Nishiyama, Kazuto Fukuchi, Youhei Akimoto, Jun Sakuma

papers.title: Low Rank Matrix Completion via Robust Alternating Minimization in Nearly Linear Time
papers.summary: Given a matrix $M\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, the low rank matrix completion problem asks us to find a rank-$k$ approximation of $M$ as $UV^\top$ for $U\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$ and $V\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ by only observing a few entries specified by a set of entries $\Omega\subseteq [m]\times [n]$. In particular, we examine an approach that is widely used in practice -- the alternating minimization framework. Jain, Netrapalli, and Sanghavi [JNS13] showed that if $M$ has incoherent rows and columns, then alternating minimization provably recovers the matrix $M$ by observing a nearly linear in $n$ number of entries. While the sample complexity has been subsequently improved [GLZ17], alternating minimization steps are required to be computed exactly. This hinders the development of more efficient algorithms and fails to depict the practical implementation of alternating minimization, where the updates are usually performed approximately in favor of efficiency. In this paper, we take a major step towards a more efficient and error-robust alternating minimization framework. To this end, we develop an analytical framework for alternating minimization that can tolerate a moderate amount of errors caused by approximate updates. Moreover, our algorithm runs in time $\widetilde O(|\Omega| k)$, which is nearly linear in the time to verify the solution while preserving the sample complexity. This improves upon all prior known alternating minimization approaches which require $\widetilde O(|\Omega| k^2)$ time.

authors.name: Yuzhou Gu, Zhao Song, Junze Yin, Lichen Zhang

papers.title: Efficient Alternating Minimization with Applications to Weighted Low Rank Approximation
papers.summary: Weighted low rank approximation is a fundamental problem in numerical linear algebra, and it has many applications in machine learning. Given a matrix $M \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, a non-negative weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n \times n}$, a parameter $k$, the goal is to output two matrices $X,Y\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$ such that $\| W \circ (M - X Y^\top) \|_F$ is minimized, where $\circ$ denotes the Hadamard product. It naturally generalizes the well-studied low rank matrix completion problem. Such a problem is known to be NP-hard and even hard to approximate assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis [GG11, RSW16]. Meanwhile, alternating minimization is a good heuristic solution for weighted low rank approximation. In particular, [LLR16] shows that, under mild assumptions, alternating minimization does provide provable guarantees. In this work, we develop an efficient and robust framework for alternating minimization that allows the alternating updates to be computed approximately. For weighted low rank approximation, this improves the cost of each iteration of [LLR16] from $\|W\|_0k^2$ to $\|W\|_0 k$ where $\|W\|_0$ denotes the number of nonzero entries of the weight matrix. At the heart of our framework is a high-accuracy multiple response regression solver together with a robust analysis of alternating minimization. We also replace the random initialization of [LLR16], whose claimed guarantee fails, by subspace iteration from a Gaussian start, so our total running time of $\widetilde O((\|W\|_0 k+nk^3)\log(1/\epsilon))$ includes the initialization. In exchange, our guarantee needs the weight matrix to be within spectral distance $\gamma n$ of the all-ones matrix for a $\gamma$ that is polynomially small in $n$.

authors.name: Zhao Song, Mingquan Ye, Junze Yin, Lichen Zhang

papers.title: FedADMM-InSa: An Inexact and Self-Adaptive ADMM for Federated Learning
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) is a promising framework for learning from distributed data while maintaining privacy. The development of efficient FL algorithms encounters various challenges, including heterogeneous data and systems, limited communication capacities, and constrained local computational resources. Recently developed FedADMM methods show great resilience to both data and system heterogeneity. However, they still suffer from performance deterioration if the hyperparameters are not carefully tuned. To address this issue, we propose an inexact and self-adaptive FedADMM algorithm, termed FedADMM-InSa. First, we design an inexactness criterion for the clients' local updates to eliminate the need for empirically setting the local training accuracy. This inexactness criterion can be assessed by each client independently based on its unique condition, thereby reducing the local computational cost and mitigating the undesirable straggle effect. The convergence of the resulting inexact ADMM is proved under the assumption of strongly convex loss functions. Additionally, we present a self-adaptive scheme that dynamically adjusts each client's penalty parameter, enhancing algorithm robustness by mitigating the need for empirical penalty parameter choices for each client. Extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets are conducted. As validated by some numerical tests, our proposed algorithm can reduce the clients' local computational load significantly and also accelerate the learning process compared to the vanilla FedADMM. The source code is available at https://github.com/DCN-FAU-AvH/FedADMM-InSa.

authors.name: Yongcun Song, Ziqi Wang, Enrique Zuazua

papers.title: Hybrid FedGraph: An efficient hybrid federated learning algorithm using graph convolutional neural network
papers.summary: Federated learning is an emerging paradigm for decentralized training of machine learning models on distributed clients, without revealing the data to the central server. Most existing works have focused on horizontal or vertical data distributions, where each client possesses different samples with shared features, or each client fully shares only sample indices, respectively. However, the hybrid scheme is much less studied, even though it is much more common in the real world. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a generalized algorithm, FedGraph, that introduces a graph convolutional neural network to capture feature-sharing information while learning features from a subset of clients. We also develop a simple but effective clustering algorithm that aggregates features produced by the deep neural networks of each client while preserving data privacy.

authors.name: Jaeyeon Jang, Diego Klabjan, Veena Mendiratta, Fanfei Meng

papers.title: Improving Graph Out-of-distribution Generalization Beyond Causality
papers.summary: Existing methods for graph out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization primarily rely on empirical studies on synthetic datasets. Such approaches tend to overemphasize the causal relationships between invariant sub-graphs and labels, thereby neglecting the non-negligible role of environment in real-world scenarios. In contrast to previous studies that impose rigid independence assumptions on environments and invariant sub-graphs, this paper presents the theorems of environment-label dependency and mutable rationale invariance, where the former characterizes the usefulness of environments in determining graph labels while the latter refers to the mutable importance of graph rationales. Based on analytic investigations, a novel variational inference based method named ``Probability Dependency on Environments and Rationales for OOD Graphs on Real-world Data'' (DEROG) is introduced. To alleviate the adverse effect of unknown prior knowledge on environments and rationales, DEROG utilizes generalized Bayesian inference. Further, DEROG employs an EM-based algorithm for optimization. Finally, extensive experiments on real-world datasets under different distribution shifts are conducted to show the superiority of DEROG. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LEOXC1571/DEROG.

authors.name: Can Xu, Yao Cheng, Jianxiang Yu, Haosen Wang, Jingsong Lv, Yao Liu, Xiang Li

papers.title: Hessian-Informed Flow Matching
papers.summary: Data from physical systems often concentrate near stable states corresponding to minima of an energy function. Around these states, the curvature of the energy landscape shapes the local covariance structure of the data, which is often highly anisotropic: small perturbations around a data point raise its energy more sharply in some directions than in others. However, standard flow matching commonly connects noise to target data through isotropic conditional paths that do not explicitly follow this physical structure. We introduce Hessian-Informed Flow Matching (HI-FM), which uses the energy Hessian at each data sample to encode this local curvature in the conditional probability paths used for training. By locally linearizing energy-driven dynamics, we derive anisotropic paths that move samples toward their targets at different rates in different directions, without changing the standard flow matching objective. We evaluate HI-FM through molecular generation on Hessian-QM9 and GEOM-Drugs, using SemlaFlow as a shared backbone. With Hessians calculated offline only for the training data, across both datasets, HI-FM improves the physical and geometric quality of generated molecules while maintaining comparable chemical validity. Under a matched optimizer-update budget, HI-FM trained with only $10\%$ of Hessian-QM9 achieves lower mean energy, strain, and bond-length $W_1$ than the full-data SemlaFlow baseline. The results support local energy curvature as a useful inductive bias for flow matching.

authors.name: Christopher Iliffe Sprague, Mert Can Kurucu, Riccardo Tedoldi, Alessandro Tibo, Jon Paul Janet, Hossein Azizpour

papers.title: From Models To Experiments: Shallow Recurrent Decoder Networks on the DYNASTY Experimental Facility
papers.summary: The Shallow Recurrent Decoder networks are a novel paradigm recently introduced for state estimation, combining sparse observations with high-dimensional model data. This architecture features important advantages compared to standard data-driven methods including: the ability to use only three sensors (even randomly selected) for reconstructing the entire dynamics of a physical system; the ability to train on compressed data spanned by a reduced basis; the ability to measure a single field variable (easy to measure) and reconstruct coupled spatio-temporal fields that are not observable and minimal hyper-parameter tuning. This approach has been verified on different test cases within different fields including nuclear reactors, even though an application to a real experimental facility, adopting the employment of in-situ observed quantities, is missing. This work aims to fill this gap by applying the Shallow Recurrent Decoder architecture to the DYNASTY facility, built at Politecnico di Milano, which studies the natural circulation established by internally heated fluids for Generation IV applications, especially in the case of Circulating Fuel reactors. The RELAP5 code is used to generate the high-fidelity data, and temperature measurements extracted by the facility are used as input for the state estimation. The results of this work will provide a validation of the Shallow Recurrent Decoder architecture to engineering systems, showing the capabilities of this approach to provide and accurate state estimation.

authors.name: Stefano Riva, Andrea Missaglia, Carolina Introini, J. Nathan Kutz, Antonio Cammi

papers.title: Refining Few-Step Text-to-Multiview Diffusion via Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Text-to-multiview (T2MV) diffusion models have shown great promise in generating multiple views of a scene from a single text prompt. While few-step backbones enable real-time T2MV generation, they often compromise key aspects of generation quality, such as per-view fidelity and cross-view consistency. Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning offers a potential solution, yet existing approaches designed for single-image diffusion do not readily extend to the few-step T2MV setting, as they neglect cross-view coordination and suffer from weak learning signals in few-step regimes. To address this, we propose MVC-ZigAL, a tailored RL finetuning framework for few-step T2MV diffusion models. Specifically, its core insights are: (1) a new MDP formulation that jointly models all generated views and assesses their collective quality via a joint-view reward; (2) a novel advantage learning strategy that exploits the performance gains of a self-refinement sampling scheme over standard sampling, yielding stronger learning signals for effective RL finetuning; and (3) a unified RL framework that extends advantage learning with a Lagrangian dual formulation for multiview-constrained optimization, balancing single-view and joint-view objectives through adaptive primal-dual updates under a self-paced threshold curriculum that harmonizes exploration and constraint enforcement. Collectively, these designs enable robust and balanced RL finetuning for few-step T2MV diffusion models, yielding substantial gains in both per-view fidelity and cross-view consistency. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyiZhang27/MVC-ZigAL.

authors.name: Ziyi Zhang, Li Shen, Deheng Ye, Yong Luo, Huangxuan Zhao, Meng Liu, Wei Yu, Lefei Zhang

papers.title: Diffusion Guidance Is a Controllable Policy Improvement Operator
papers.summary: At the core of reinforcement learning is the idea of learning beyond the performance in the data. However, scaling such systems has proven notoriously tricky. In contrast, techniques from generative modeling have proven remarkably scalable and are simple to train. In this work, we combine these strengths, by deriving a direct relation between policy improvement and guidance of diffusion models. The resulting framework, CFGRL, is trained with the simplicity of supervised learning, yet can further improve on the policies in the data. On offline RL tasks, we observe a reliable trend -- increased guidance weighting leads to increased performance. Of particular importance, CFGRL can operate without explicitly learning a value function, allowing us to generalize simple supervised methods (e.g., goal-conditioned behavioral cloning) to further prioritize optimality, gaining performance for "free" across the board.

authors.name: Kevin Frans, Seohong Park, Pieter Abbeel, Sergey Levine

papers.title: On Designing Diffusion Autoencoders for Efficient Generation and Representation Learning
papers.summary: Diffusion autoencoders (DAs) are variants of diffusion models that use an input-dependent latent variable to capture representations alongside the diffusion process. The latent variable is typically used for tasks such as downstream classification, controllable generation, and interpolation. However, the latent variable has an effect on unconditional generation, with performance strongly dependent on how this variable is modelled and learnt and how it is used in the denoising process. Here, we draw a connection between DAs and a particular class of improved diffusion models---those that learn their forward (noising) process---to argue that DAs have unrealised potential as generative models. We develop a variant of DAs, termed diffusion models with $z$ (DMZ), to show that the adoption of certain design decisions, such as the choice of latent variables and conditioning method, can help realise this generative potential. Through extensive experiments and ablations, we show DMZ converges in fewer iterations, generates high-quality samples with fewer denoising steps, and learns effective latent representations for downstream tasks like classification and domain transfer.

authors.name: Magdalena Proszewska, Esmeralda S. Whitammer, N. Siddharth

papers.title: Quantum Geometry of Data
papers.summary: We demonstrate how Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML) encodes data as quantum geometry. In QCML, features of the data are represented by learned Hermitian matrices, and data points are mapped to states in Hilbert space. The quantum geometry description endows the dataset with rich geometric and topological structure---including intrinsic dimension, quantum metric, and Berry curvature---derived directly from the data. QCML captures global properties of data through a compact operator representation. At fixed Hilbert-space dimension, the number of operator parameters grows only linearly with the number of features. The present work provides the first full exposition of QCML as a framework for matrix geometry, establishing its mathematical foundation and demonstrating how operator-level tools from quantum geometry can be directly applied to data. We introduce the matrix Laplacian and its eigenmaps as a geometry-preserving alternative to graph-based embeddings, and we show how topological invariants such as Chern numbers can be extracted from data for the first time. An important practical outcome is the efficiency of the representation: the relevant geometric structure of high-dimensional datasets can be captured with Hilbert spaces of size as small as $N \sim 10$. We illustrate these results on a number of synthetic and real-world examples, including the Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset, where QCML uncovers geometric separability between benign and malignant samples and yields an interpretable decomposition of feature relevance. The emphasis of this work is on a new geometric representation of data rather than on algorithmic benchmarking, establishing a foundation for extracting global geometric and topological structure from high-dimensional datasets.

authors.name: Alexander G. Abanov, Luca Candelori, Harold C. Steinacker, Martin T. Wells, Jerome R. Busemeyer, Cameron J. Hogan, Vahagn Kirakosyan, Nicola Marzari, Sunil Pinnamaneni, Dario Villani, Mengjia Xu, Kharen Musaelian

papers.title: When Graph Structure Provably Helps Classification: Non-Asymptotic Recovery Guarantees
papers.summary: The joint use of graph structure and node-specific information is central to transductive node classification, yet a fundamental theoretical question remains: when does graph structure actually help? We provide the first deterministic, non-asymptotic, distribution-free answer to this question. We build on nuclear-norm graph clustering and generalized convex clustering. Our formulation of the latter incorporates node features, partial labels, and general convex loss functions, making it suitable for transductive node classification. We analyze each problem separately to characterize when graph structure alone, or node information alone, is sufficient for perfect recovery. We then formulate a unified convex optimization problem through a shared atomic norm representation and prove that combining the two sources expands the range of conditions under which perfect recovery is guaranteed beyond what either source alone can certify. This shows when node information can improve clustering and graph structure can improve classification.

authors.name: Firooz Shahriari-Mehr, Javad Aliakbari, Alexandre Graell i Amat, Ashkan Panahi

papers.title: costream: A Streaming Evaluation Protocol for Wearable Fall Detection
papers.summary: Wearable fall detectors are commonly evaluated on presegmented windows, where a fall window is extracted at an annotated impact and non-fall windows are sampled from fall-free signal. However, a deployed detector processes a continuous sensor stream in which the location of a fall is unknown. We specify a streaming evaluation protocol in which a detector traverses an unsegmented recording, aggregates window-level scores into a temporal confidence map, and emits timestamped events that are evaluated against the annotated fall. Holding the dataset, participant-wise splits, window construction and fitted models fixed, we compare presegmented and streaming evaluation on clinically verified real-world falls. The two protocols identify the same best-performing method overall, but select different methods in 6 of 20 model-window configurations, with the divergence associated with differences in the temporal clustering of false alarms. Streaming evaluation also exposes deployment-relevant quantities, including false alarm rate over elapsed monitoring time, detection delay, and the effect of the decision threshold, that are not captured by per-window evaluation. These results show that evaluation protocol can materially affect conclusions about wearable fall detectors and should be considered when assessing their suitability for continuous monitoring.

authors.name: Timilehin B. Aderinola, Ilaria D'Ascanio, Luca Palmerini, Lorenzo Chiari, Jochen Klenk, Clemens Becker, Brian Caulfield, Georgiana Ifrim

papers.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Just Classification and a Few Regressions
papers.summary: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to recover a reward function from observed behavior, but rewards are typically only partially identified: many reward--value pairs can induce the same behavior policy. We study this problem in the maximum-entropy, or Gumbel-shock, model under a broad class of statewise affine normalization constraints, with anchor-action constraints as a special case. This leads to Generalized Policy-to-$Q$-to-Reward (GenPQR), a modular approach to normalized reward recovery based on policy estimation and $Q$-evaluation via the Bellman equation; both components can be instantiated with off-the-shelf classification and regression methods. We establish modular finite-sample guarantees under general function approximation, with separate terms for policy-estimation and $Q$-function estimation error. We also give explicit bounds for GenPQR with fitted $Q$-evaluation. In experiments, GenPQR improves on DeepPQR in reward recovery. Our guarantees extend beyond anchor actions, accommodate large action spaces, and are not tied to a specific neural-network architecture or training procedure.

authors.name: Lars van der Laan, Nathan Kallus, Aurelien Bibaut

papers.title: ActiNet: An Open-Source Tool for Activity Intensity Classification of Wrist-Worn Accelerometry Using Self-Supervised Deep Learning
papers.summary: The use of accurate and reliable open-source human activity recognition (HAR) models on passively collected wrist-accelerometer data is essential in large-scale epidemiological studies that investigate the association between physical activity and health outcomes. While self-supervised learning has generated considerable excitement in improving HAR, the extent to which these models, coupled with hidden Markov models (HMMs), would make a tangible improvement to classification performance and the effect this may have on the predicted daily activity intensity compositions is unknown. Using up to 24 hours of wrist-worn accelerometer data from 151 CAPTURE-24 participants (aged 18-91, mean age 42, 66% female), we trained the ActiNet model, consisting of HARNet, a self-supervised, 18-layer, modified ResNet-V2 model, followed by hidden Markov model (HMM) smoothing, to classify labels of activity intensity. The performance of this model, evaluated using 5-fold stratified group cross-validation, was then compared to a baseline random forest (RF) + HMM, established in existing literature. Differences in performance and classification outputs were compared with different subgroups of age and sex within the CAPTURE-24 population. The ActiNet model was able to distinguish labels of activity intensity with a mean macro F1 score of 0.80 and a mean Cohen's kappa score of 0.85. This exceeded the performance of the RF + HMM, trained and validated on the same dataset, with mean scores of 0.76 and 0.80, respectively. The improvements in performance were consistent across subgroups of age and sex. These findings encourage the use of ActiNet for the extraction of activity intensity labels from wrist-accelerometer data in future epidemiological studies.

authors.name: Aidan Acquah, Shing Chan, Aiden Doherty

papers.title: CS-54k: A Paper-Grounded Corpus and Benchmark for AI Research QA
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to support computer science research. To contribute reliably, these systems must be able to work with information distributed across research papers and across different aspects of the research process. However, large-scale resources that systematically organize such information into structured supervision for both model evaluation and post-training remain limited. To address this gap, we propose a systematic paper-to-QA construction pipeline that organizes information from AI research papers into structured QA pairs supported by source evidence. Using this pipeline, we construct CS-54k, a 54k-pair corpus derived from 14,474 openly licensed AI research papers. The corpus covers eight recurring paper components, including research domain, prior work, existing challenges, motivation, findings and assumptions, methods, experimental settings, and experimental results. We further derive two complementary subsets: CS-4k, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on paper-derived research QA, and CS-50k, a companion corpus for post-training. Extensive evaluations on CS-4k reveal substantial performance differences across existing LLMs and paper components, with experimental settings and results remaining particularly challenging. Moreover, post-training on CS-50k substantially improves Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on CS-4k, demonstrating the practical utility of structured, paper-derived supervision. Together, CS-4k and CS-50k provide a unified and scalable resource for benchmarking and improving LLMs on research paper question answering.

authors.name: Penghao Wang, Yuhao Zhou, Mengxuan Wu, Ziheng Qin, Bangyuan Zhu, Shengbin Huang, Xuanlei Zhao, Panpan Zhang, Xiaojiang Peng, Yuzhang Shang, Jianfei Yang, Zheng Zhu, Tianlong Chen, Zhangyang Wang, Kai Wang

papers.title: Capturing Intransitive Dominance in Tennis Forecasting: A Graph Neural Network Approach
papers.summary: Intransitive player dominance, where player A beats B, B beats C, but C beats A, is common in competitive tennis. Yet, there are few known attempts to incorporate it within forecasting methods. We address this problem with a graph neural network approach that explicitly models these intransitive relationships through temporal directed graphs, with players as nodes and their historical match outcomes as directed edges. Our model (65.7% accuracy, 0.214 Brier score) forecasts competitively with established rating systems such as Weighted Elo. Although it does not improve on the baseline in unconditional accuracy, a forecast-encompassing test shows that it carries complementary information. A combined forecast significantly outperforms Weighted Elo, and there is some indication that the gain is larger on the intransitive matchups our model targets. A graph-based representation of player interactions thus captures a forecasting signal that transitive rating systems discard, even between players who share no common opponents.

authors.name: Lawrence Clegg, John Cartlidge

papers.title: Next-Latent Prediction Transformers Learn Compact World Models
papers.summary: Transformers replace recurrence with a memory that grows with sequence length and self-attention that enables ad-hoc lookups over past tokens. Consequently, they lack an inherent incentive to compress history into compact latent states with consistent transition rules. This often leads to learning solutions that generalize poorly. We introduce Next-Latent Prediction (NextLat), which extends standard next-token training with self-supervised predictions in the latent space. Specifically, NextLat trains a transformer to learn latent representations that are predictive of its next latent state given the next token. Theoretically, we show that these latents converge towards belief states, compressed information about the history necessary to predict the future. This simple auxiliary objective injects a recurrent inductive bias into transformers while leaving their architecture, parallel training efficiency, and inference unchanged. NextLat effectively encourages transformers to form compact internal world models with coherent belief states and transition dynamics -- crucial properties not guaranteed by standard next-token prediction alone. Empirically, across benchmarks in world modeling, reasoning, planning, and language modeling, NextLat demonstrates significant gains over standard next-token prediction and other baselines in downstream accuracy, representation compression, and lookahead planning. Furthermore, NextLat enables variable-length self-speculative decoding, accelerating inference by up to 3.3x in language modeling. NextLat offers a simple yet effective paradigm for learning compact, predictive representations in transformers that generalize better. Our code is available at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/NextLat.

authors.name: Jayden Teoh, Manan Tomar, Kwangjun Ahn, Edward S. Hu, Tim Pearce, Pratyusha Sharma, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Riashat Islam, Alex Lamb, John Langford

papers.title: Convergence and stability of Q-learning in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning promises, among other benefits, to efficiently capture and utilize the temporal structure of a decision-making problem and to enhance transfer learning capabilities, but theoretical guarantees lag behind practice. In this paper, we propose a Feudal Q-learning scheme and investigate under which conditions its coupled updates converge and are stable. By leveraging the theory of Stochastic Approximation and the ODE method, we present a theorem stating the convergence and stability properties of Feudal Q-learning. This provides a principled convergence and stability analysis tailored to Feudal RL. Moreover, we show that the updates converge to a point that can be interpreted as an equilibrium of a suitably defined game, opening the door to game-theoretic approaches to Hierarchical RL. Lastly, experiments based on the Feudal Q-learning algorithm support the outcomes anticipated by theory.

authors.name: Massimiliano Manenti, Andrea Iannelli

papers.title: Critical Organization of p-Adic Deep Neural Networks
papers.summary: We study continuous neural networks whose neurons are the points of the ring of p-adic integers, a fractal tree-like space that encodes hierarchical architectures. The hidden states solve a nonlinear integral equation, which describes the equilibria of recurrent networks and deep equilibrium models; feedforward architectures appear as the special case of kernels without feedback. We prove that the state is unique and depends Lipschitz-continuously on the parameters whenever the product of the Lipschitz constant of the activation function and the operator norm of the connectivity is less than one, and that, when the parameters are locally constant, every state is exactly the state of a finite network with a tree-like topology. We introduce p-adic discrete deep networks, whose layers are the levels of the tree and whose weights are coarse-grainings of a single kernel, and show that, in the stable region, they converge to the continuous network as the depth tends to infinity. Feedforward networks always have a unique state; hence a multiplicity of states, and therefore critical organization in our sense, requires recurrence. For recurrent networks with radial kernels we prove a sharp transition: the zero state is the only state if and only if the total coupling does not exceed one. For hierarchical kernels, above the threshold, the states are indexed by sign patterns on the leaves of the tree, their number is computed exactly, and they form a tree-indexed partially ordered set graded by instability. Numerical experiments illustrate these results and test conjectures on general radial kernels and on random recurrent networks on the tree. Finally, we interpret the critical organization hypothesis for deep neural networks, originally formulated for brain organization, through the lens of multistability, and we discuss the continuous limits of families of finite networks.

authors.name: W. A. Z\'u\~niga-Galindo

papers.title: Spectral Ghost in Representation Learning: A Unified View from Component Analysis to Self-Supervised Learning
papers.summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) extracts representations from massive unlabeled data that transfer to a variety of downstream tasks. Its empirical success has produced a dizzying array of objectives and procedures, yet a clear understanding of what representation is desired, and why these seemingly different methods work, is still missing. In this paper, we develop a unified spectral framework for representation learning. We first show that a representation is sufficient for arbitrary downstream prediction with a linear head if it spans the spectral decomposition of the pointwise mutual information, which can be extracted purely from unlabeled data. This view organizes representation learning along two axes, the parametrization of the spectral representation (linear, energy-based, denoising, nonlinear, latent-variable, and multi-modal) and the learning objective for fitting it, under which a broad range of existing methods, including SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, Barlow Twins, VICReg, DINO, MAE, JEPA, BERT, GPT, and CLIP, as well as classic PCA, CCA, Laplacian eigenmaps, LLE, and SNE, are recovered as particular combinations. The framework also clarifies optimization behaviors: the batch-size requirement is determined by whether the objective is unbiased, a consistent surrogate, or biased, rather than by contrastive vs. non-contrastive losses. Finally, the framework inspires new scalable algorithms and extends spectral representations to causal inference and reinforcement learning.

authors.name: Bo Dai, Na Li, Dale Schuurmans

papers.title: Graph-Free Root Cause Analysis
papers.summary: Failures in complex systems demand rapid Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to prevent cascading damage. Graph-free RCA methods typically assume that the root cause has the highest anomaly score. This assumption fails when faults propagate, because a small deviation at the root cause can grow into a larger anomaly downstream. Our key observation is that a root cause deviates in both its internal properties (e.g., resource usage) and external properties (e.g., latency), whereas components affected by propagation deviate only in external properties. We propose CIE, a framework that ranks components by combining their internal and external anomaly scores. We formalize a class of component-based systems and state conditions under which CIE provably ranks the root cause first. The guarantee holds under arbitrary amplification for a conjunctive score, and under bounded amplification and a stronger root-cause condition for the default additive score. On 735 failures in nine datasets from three microservice systems, CIE achieves 68% Top-1 accuracy averaged over 11 fault types, a 21% relative improvement over the best of twelve baselines, while requiring 8 ms per diagnosis.

authors.name: Luan Pham

papers.title: Understanding and Learning Prediction Targets in Diffusion Models
