We consider an ideal SBR, which reflects 100% of non-harvestable low-energy photons but does not alter the reflectivity of the PV module for usable high-energy photons, and estimate how reducing the module temperature with the SBR affects the annual and the cumulative energy yield of silicon PV modules for six locations in North America and Europe. An ideal SBR would increase the annual energy yield between 0.9% and 1.4% for open-rack mounted modules and between 1.5% and 2.3% for close-roof mounted PV modules. Whether a non-ideal SBR provides a benefit in actual deployments strongly depends on the location and the optical properties of the coating. Beyond effects on the instantaneous power conversion efficiency and hence the annual energy yield, reducing the temperature by an SBR might also reduce the degradation and increase the overall lifetime of the PV module. By describing degradation using a simple Arrhenius approach with typical activation energies between 0.4 eV and 0.8 eV, we find that an ideal SBR increases the cumulative energy yield over 30 years between 2.2% and 4.0% for an open-rack mounted PV module in Princeton, New Jersey, USA.

authors.name: Klaus J\"ager, Jyotirmoy Mandal, Barry P. Rand, Forrest Meggers, Christiane Becker

papers.title: When Should Science Act on an Interstellar Anomaly?
papers.summary: An unusual interstellar object may warrant further observation even when there is little evidence that it is artificial. The challenge is deciding which observations are worth pursuing, how much to invest in them, and when to stop. We argue that the Loeb Scale can help guide these decisions, provided its levels are understood as provisional assessments rather than estimates of the probability of extraterrestrial technology. Candidate technosignature status may justify targeted follow-up when new observations could distinguish competing explanations and the expected scientific value warrants the cost. This requires testable predictions and retrodictions, attention to natural explanations not yet considered, and recognition of the risks of false alarms. We place this argument in the broader history and philosophy of scientific anomalies and relate it to existing assessment frameworks in SETI and astrobiology. The cases of 1I/Oumuamua, 2I/Borisov, and 3I/ATLAS illustrate why classifications and research priorities must remain open to revision. Candidate status is a reason to seek better evidence while it can still be obtained, not a conclusion about an object's origin.

authors.name: Konrad Szocik, Abraham Loeb

papers.title: Lagrangian single-particle, multi-particle and topological analyses in turbulent Rayleigh-B\'enard convection
papers.summary: We present 3d Lagrangian DNS of turbulent RBC for $Pr=0.7$, spanning $10^5\leq Ra\leq10^{10}$ in a laterally periodic domain of $\Gamma=4$, complemented by dense multi-particle cloud simulations for $10^4\leq Ra\leq 10^8$ at $\Gamma=16$. Using single-particle accelerations, Lagrangian heat transfer, Q-R invariant topology, pair dispersion, scale-dependent Lagrangian eddy viscosity, and principal component analysis of particle clouds, we establish a hierarchical, scale-bridging framework of convective transport. Controlling spectral-element signatures via cubic smoothing splines yields highly intermittent distributions and Heisenberg-Yaglom scaling in the core, while a mixed viscous-thermal model reveals that thermal dissipation significantly drives vertical bulk and horizontal boundary-layer accelerations. Evaluating exact local temperature gradients along tracer trajectories reveals extreme intermittency, where particles carry convective heat fluxes up to 250 times the global Eulerian mean. Dust-devil-like convective vortices, isolated via an ANOVA-validated filtering algorithm at $Ra=10^{10}$, dominate the vortex-stretching quadrant of the Q-R invariant map and drive local heat transfer up to 30 times the global Eulerian mean. Our results do not support a Bolgiano-Obukhov (BO59) cascade in the Lagrangian frame. Complementing pair dispersion with scale-dependent Lagrangian eddy viscosity isolates initial-separation and viscous catch-up effects at the viscous-to-inertial crossover, revealing an extended Richardson shoulder and bulk behaviour increasingly reminiscent of HIT with rising $Ra$. Analysing particle clouds via logarithmic shape invariants, MSD, and the logarithmic geometric mean radius extends this picture to 3d Richardson-like volumetric expansion, showing that plume entrainment induces uniaxial stretching that reduces kinematic catch-up rather than sustaining a BO59 cascade.

authors.name: Matti Ettel, Roshan J. Samuel, Michael Chertkov, J\"org Schumacher

papers.title: Role of Metastable Dicationic Intermediates in the Breakup of CH$_4^{2+}$
papers.summary: We investigate the fragmentation dynamics of methane dication (CH$_4^{2+}$) produced in collisions with 50-MeV C$^{6+}$ ions using the COLTRIMS technique. The method provides complete three-dimensional momentum vectors of the charged fragments, enabling full kinematic reconstruction of the fragmentation process. The dynamics are analyzed using Dalitz plots, Newton diagrams, and the native-frame method to distinguish between concerted and sequential dissociation mechanisms. The data indicate the presence of sequential fragmentation pathways for the CH$_4^{2+}$ $\rightarrow$ CH$_2^+$ + H$^+$ + H, CH$_4^{2+}$ $\rightarrow$ CH$^+$ + H$^+$ + 2H, and CH$_4^{2+}$ $\rightarrow$ C$^+$ + H$^+$ + 3H channels, consistent with dissociation via short-lived dicationic intermediates CH$_3^{2+}$, CH$_2^{2+}$, and CH$^{2+}$, respectively. From the Newton-diagram momentum distributions, we estimate half-rotational periods of approximately 180~fs, 71~fs, and 44~fs for the $\mathrm{CH_3^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{CH_2^{2+}}$, and $\mathrm{CH^{2+}}$ intermediates, respectively, providing characteristic lower-limit timescales for their survival prior to fragmentation. The experimental observations are further supported by comparisons with calculated potential-energy curves.

authors.name: Samiksha Dehru, Evan Munaro-Langlo\"ys, Aditya Yadav, Siddhanta Barnowal, Manojit Das, Harpreet Singh, Jibak Mukherjee, Rajarshi Sinha-Roy, Victor Despr\'e, Deepankar Misra, Arnab Khan

papers.title: Two-way coupling of gravity waves and wind farm wakes: a reduced-order boundary-layer model
papers.summary: This paper develops a reduced-order numerical framework for modelling the two-way coupling between gravity waves and turbulent wakes in large-scale wind farms. Starting with the non-hydrostatic Boussinesq equations and introducing simplifications appropriate to the boundary layer and the overlying stratified free atmosphere yield separate governing equations for the two regions. These are coupled through a dynamic boundary condition at the capping inversion, which directly captures the feedback of gravity waves on the boundary-layer flow. A mixed pseudo-spectral finite-difference discretisation yields a computationally efficient model while retaining vertical boundary-layer structure. For the semi-infinite wind farm considered here, a complete solution is obtained in a matter of seconds on a standard laptop. Comparisons with large-eddy simulations (LES) confirm the model successfully reproduces both internal wind-farm flow and large-scale gravity-wave effects. It captures the upstream blockage induced by adverse pressure gradients, as well as the accelerated wake recovery within and downwind of the farm, driven by favourable pressure gradients.

authors.name: Hossein A. Kafiabad, Majid Bastankhah

papers.title: Independent amplitude and phase modulation using two sequential regions of one phase-only SLM
papers.summary: Liquid-crystal spatial light modulators (SLMs) are widely used for programmable wavefront control but are typically operated as phase-only devices, limiting applications that require independent amplitude and phase shaping. Here we demonstrate full complex-field modulation using a single phase-only SLM by implementing two sequential modulation planes on different regions of the same device. The phase retardance introduced by the first SLM region is converted into amplitude modulation by a polarizer placed in the beam path, while the second region compensates the associated phase offset and imposes the required phase distribution. The field from the first region is imaged onto the second, enabling complex-field synthesis without a second modulator. We validate the approach by generating Bessel--Gaussian beams, helical-phase fields, and arbitrary focal-plane intensity patterns. This single-SLM platform provides a compact route to programmable complex wavefront engineering for structured illumination, holography, and electron--light interaction experiments.

authors.name: Marius Constantin Chirita Mihaila, Mikul\'a\v{s} Fiala, Martin Koz\'ak

papers.title: GPU Acceleration of Collinear and Noncollinear DFT Using a Numerical Atomic Orbital-Based DFT Code
papers.summary: We implement GPU acceleration of collinear and noncollinear density functional theory (DFT) calculations in the numerical atomic orbitals (NAOs) code OpenMX by offloading matrix multiplications and eigenvalue solves (plus selected auxiliary steps) to cuBLAS/cuSOLVER and OpenACC. Benchmarks on the Pegasus supercomputer (per node: a 48-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 CPU and one NVIDIA H100 GPU) compare GPU-accelerated and CPU-only runs under identical settings. For a 512-atom collinear case on two nodes (two GPUs total), the GPU-accelerated calculation achieves a 2.02 times speedup over a CPU-only run on two nodes (96 CPU cores total); for a 384-atom noncollinear case on two nodes (two GPUs total), the speedup is 2.60 times over two CPU-only nodes (96 cores). These results demonstrate practical GPU-accelerated DFT in an NAO-based code for both collinear and noncollinear calculations.

authors.name: Hiroyuki Kawai (Department of Physics, Niigata University), Takuya Sekikawa (Nuclear Science and Engineering Center, Japan Atomic Energy Agency), Taisuke Ozaki (Institute for Solid State Physics, The University of Tokyo), Yoshiaki \=Ono (Department of Physics, Niigata University)

papers.title: Data-driven surrogate models for forecasting experimentally measured fluid flows
papers.summary: Data-driven modeling shows significant promise for faster-than-real-time forecasting of fluid flows. For real-world engineering applications (e.g., flow control), models must contend with limited, imperfect, and incomplete experimental measurements. In this work, we present an analysis of data-driven surrogate models trained to forecast the time-evolution of experimentally measured cylinder wakes in the subcritical vortex shedding regime. Using a dataset of two-dimensional, two-component particle image velocimetry measurements, we train fully convolutional neural networks, U-Nets, Fourier neural operators, and dynamic mode decomposition-based models to forecast the development of experimentally measured velocity fields. To characterize data-driven approaches contending with transient flow features and limited, imperfect observations, the development of predictions over extended forecast horizons is examined at a fixed Reynolds number (Re = 590). Next, models are trained at a range of Reynolds numbers (Re = 230 to Re = 2920) to investigate the impact of increasingly turbulent and three-dimensional flow phenomena, and the challenges associated with measuring them, on forecast quality. We find that experimentally trained surrogate models can provide meaningful predictions over short time horizons, propagate low-frequency dynamics over longer forecast periods, and achieve faster-than-real-time evaluation. However, the data-driven models struggle to preserve transient flow features and high-frequency energy content when faced with noisy measurements and incomplete state observations. This emphasizes the underlying challenges that remain for data-driven modeling approaches to effectively contend with fluid dynamics in real-world engineering applications, where observations are often imperfect and limited.

authors.name: Peter I. Renn, Emily H. Palmer, Cong Wang, Morteza Gharib

papers.title: White-Light Matter-Wave Interferometry
papers.summary: White-light interferometry exploits broadband optical spectra to generate a localized interference envelope, providing a unique reference beyond the periodicity of individual fringes and underpinning numerous applications in precision metrology, ranging, and imaging. Despite the common wave nature of light and matter, a matter-wave counterpart of white-light interferometry has remained unexplored. Here we report the first realization of white-light matter-wave interferometry, extending this established optical paradigm to matter waves. Using a continuous atomic beam as a broadband matter-wave source, we synthesize velocity-dependent spectral components to generate a localized matter-wave interference envelope, introducing a new measurement observable based on envelope localization rather than conventional fringe-phase estimation. As a proof-of-principle demonstration, we implement simultaneous dual-axis rotation and acceleration sensing with a white-light Mach--Zehnder atom interferometer, revealing three defining features: envelope localization beyond phase ambiguity, a velocity-engineered measurement response, and intrinsic rejection of phase bias. We further measure the Earth's rotation with a relative error of 4.3$\%$ and achieve a long-term stability of 93 ppm relative to the Earth's rotation rate after 15,000 s of averaging. These results establish a new interferometric mechanism in which ambiguity, measurement response, and robustness can be addressed through the intrinsic design of the broadband matter-wave interference itself, extending the principles of optical white-light interferometry to atom optics and opening new opportunities for quantum sensing, precision metrology, and matter-wave metrology.

authors.name: Wei-Chen Jia, Yue Xin, Ke Shen, Zhi-Xin Meng, Yan-Ying Feng

papers.title: Discrete phase symmetry of stationary states in bichromatically pumped Kerr microresonators
papers.summary: Bichromatically pumped Kerr microresonators can exhibit phase multistability due to four-wave mixing between the pump modes and the generated modes. Here, we analyze the symmetry structure of stationary solutions within the coupled-mode description of these systems. We show that the two-pump coupled-mode equations belong to a broader class of models with equally spaced driven modes and mode-dependent nonlinear coupling coefficients, losses, and detunings. In this generalized setting, each stationary solution generates a finite family of stationary solutions under a discrete phase transformation. For each nonzero modal amplitude, the number of distinct phase values within a symmetry orbit is determined solely by the mode index and the pump-mode spacing. We show that the phase-counting rule also applies to modes outside the interval between the two pumps, where it reproduces the symmetry observed within that interval. In addition, the same phase-multistability mechanism can arise in configurations with multiple pump modes, provided that adjacent pumps are separated by the same number of resonator modes.

authors.name: B. N. Nougmanov, V. L. Gorshenin, N. S. Tatarinova, D. A. Chermoshentsev, I. A. Bilenko, F. Y. Khalili

papers.title: Ultrashort Two-Pulse Train Generation on a 100 TW Laser Beamline Using a Delay Mask After the Final Focusing Optics
papers.summary: Experimental results showing the generation of an ultrashort two-pulse train using a two-section delay mask placed downstream of the off-axis parabola focusing optics are reported. Based on the initial simulation results, a circular fused silica plate with a central aperture and a measured thickness of $570\pm50$ $\mu$m used in the quantitative delay calculation was designed to enable two distinct transverse portions of the incident laser pulse to be focused, ideally, with equal intensity. This fulfills one of the requirements of the resonant multi-pulse ionization injection (ReMPI) scheme for laser wakefield acceleration. As an intermediary step, a calibration of Gafchromic EBT4 films against laser fluence was established, enabling direct characterization of the unattenuated transverse beam profile. The experiment was carried out at the CNR-INO Intense Laser Irradiation Laboratory (ILIL) using a 240 TW laser system operated at 100 TW as part of the ongoing preparation for the first experimental demonstration of ReMPI. The pulse-to-pulse delay introduced by the delay mask was experimentally measured (at a reduced power, as customary for temporal autocorrelation measurements) to be $\simeq 901$ fs, in good agreement with the expected value of $\simeq 888$ fs. While the pulse-to-pulse delay is not yet optimized for ReMPI operation at practically relevant plasma densities, the experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed delay-mask concept.

authors.name: David Gregocki, Luca Labate, Federica Baffigi, Lorenzo Fulgentini, Leonida Antonio Gizzi

papers.title: Modeling inhomogeneous spatial point configurations with applications to replicated patterns in real-life waiting crowds
papers.summary: In this article, we connect statistical inference for spatial point processes with the analysis of waiting pedestrian crowds through two interconnected contributions. First, on the methodological side we develop an inference procedure for semiparametric spatial point process models leveraging replicated spatial patterns, i.e., multiple approximately independent realizations from the same process. Second, we show that spatial point processes provide a suitable modeling framework for waiting pedestrians, capturing two key aspects: spatial inhomogeneity driven by location attractiveness and repulsive interactions between pedestrians. These two components are central to the inference problem itself, since spatial point process modeling hinges on disentangling background intensity from interaction. Although replicated spatial patterns are rare in point process literature, they are available here through a unique real-life pedestrian dataset, thereby directly linking the methodological development to the physical application. We use the proposed methods to fit and evaluate determinantal and Gibbs point processes in a simulation study and a real-world case study. Despite persistent challenges in decoupling the influences of inhomogeneity from interaction, these models are able to reproduce key empirical features of waiting pedestrians.

authors.name: Lars Sickert Karam, Rui M. Castro, Maarten Schoukens, Alessandro Corbetta

papers.title: Sea Surface Roughness Dependence on Ocean Wave Parameters through Large Eddy Simulation with Local Subfilter Wave Drag
papers.summary: Characterizing the Marine Atmospheric Boundary Layer (MABL) requires understanding the coupling between ocean waves and the turbulent atmospheric boundary layer above them. This coupling controls momentum exchange between the atmosphere and the ocean; it is of practical importance in the global climate, flow of ocean currents, ocean engineering, and offshore wind energy. Computational study of the MABL is complex because it must resolve the coupled physics of waves and turbulence over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. This study expands on approaches for representing dynamic, local waves in Large Eddy Simulations (LES) of the MABL by developing a subfilter wave drag model to be local and scale-invariant. It explores the effects of different wave parameters (significant wave height and peak frequency of the wave energy spectrum) on the resulting momentum flux beyond monotonic relationships between surface stress through friction velocity $u_\ast$ and wind velocity above the surface $U_{10}$. Results are compared to field data and in a discussion on how representation of the MABL and associated momentum flux need to account for both wind and wave effects.

authors.name: Hannah Hata Williams, Aditya K. Aiyer, Luc Deike, Michael E. Mueller

papers.title: Transverse Modulation of Continuous Electron Beams by a Structured Optical Cavity
papers.summary: Compact aberration correction at large semi-angles remains a central challenge in electron microscopy. Here we propose a phase plate for continuous electron beams based on the ponderomotive interaction with an intracavity standing wave in a near-concentric Fabry--P\'erot resonator. For electrons propagating along the cavity axis, a standing-wave with Laguerre-Gaussian mode of topological charge $l=1$ imprints an annular phase shift that is opposite in sign to the third-order spherical aberration of a conventional electron lens. For a \(5~\mathrm{keV}\) beam with a convergence semi-angle of \(25~\mathrm{mrad}\), we fully compensate the third-order spherical aberration of an objective lens with \(C_\mathrm{s}=1~\mathrm{mm}\), yielding the transverse width of the corrected probe in the focus of \(\sigma_\mathrm{p}=1.4~\mathrm{\AA}\). The accessible transverse electron phases are set by the supported resonator modal basis and its coherent superpositions.

authors.name: Marius Constantin Chirita Mihaila, Julie Sk{\'y}palov\'a, Martin Koz\'ak

papers.title: Scaling of the minimal energy for turbulence transition in pipe flow
papers.summary: Predicting the transition to turbulence in pipe flow remains a fundamental problem in fluid dynamics. We use a variational approach to compute nonlinear optimal perturbations to the laminar flow. Optimal perturbations are structurally similar for all Reynolds numbers, $1750 \leq Re \leq 10^4$, considered. As $Re$ increases, they increasingly localise in space with thickness scaling as $ Re^{-1/3}$. They grow via the Orr mechanism, followed by a phase of energy transfer across oblique waves of different axial wavenumber, characterised by a rapid delocalisation. The energy gain in the Orr and oblique-wave phases is independent of the initial perturbation energy, $E_0$. Subsequently, rolls grow by nonlinear mechanisms and streaks via the lift-up effect. The energy gain of the (inviscid) Orr phase is independent of the Reynolds number, whereas it increases linearly with $Re$ during the initial oblique-wave phase and quadratically in the roll and lift-up phase. We find that, transition occurs if the energy of the optimal perturbation exceeds a maximum energy threshold during its temporal evolution. This energy is given by the edge state energy and found to be independent of $Re$. As a result, the minimum perturbation energy required to cause transition in pipe flow scales as $E_0^\text{crit}\propto Re^{-3}$, which is consistent with our computation of minimal seeds. We note that insufficiently long pipes lead to an exponent of smaller magnitude and that much larger numerical resolutions are required to accurately compute the energy gain than to compute the critical threshold.

authors.name: Patrick Keuchel, Daniel Mor\'on, Marc Avila

papers.title: Hydrogen-Bond Donor-Acceptor Imbalance in Low-Frequency Terahertz Water Spectra
papers.summary: The low-frequency dielectric response of liquid water is commonly described by a dominant Debye relaxation together with additional faster contributions whose microscopic origin remains debated. Here we show that the dielectric function of water between 0.14 and 1.21 THz can be represented by a collective Debye relaxation plus a Drude-Smith term constrained to the zero-dc-conductivity limit. The Drude-Smith spectral weight increases upon heating pure H2O from 20 C to 50 C and decreases upon isotopic substitution (D2O at 20 C vs. H2O at 20 C). Molecular dynamics simulations including nuclear quantum effects show correlated changes in the population of water molecules with unequal numbers of donated and accepted hydrogen-bonds. Ab-initio-based spectra calculations further indicate that the ~0.1-1 THz response contains both nuclear-motion and explicit electronic-polarisation/charge-redistribution contributions. We therefore interpret the excess low-frequency THz response as a localised, mixed nuclear-electronic dielectric response correlated with transient donor-acceptor imbalance in the hydrogen-bond network.

authors.name: Lilian Najm Alsayed, Florian Pabst, Giuseppe Cassone, Ali Hassanali, Fabio Novelli

papers.title: The fixed boundary plasma equilibrium basis for a one Gigawatt electric stellarator power plant
papers.summary: A fixed boundary stellarator equilibrium capable of producing 3 GW of fusion power (1 GW-electric) is presented as the design basis for the GIGA fusion power plant being developed by Gauss Fusion GmbH. The stellarator concept provides a steady-state, transient free, low recirculating power approach to a fusion power plant, which builds on 50 years of progress in plasma physics. A set of requirements for a fixed boundary equilibrium were determined through application of 0.5 D modeling. Optimization of a modified Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) equilibrium was performed to achieve these requirements including alpha power confinement greater than $85\%$, neoclassical effective ripple below 0.01, bootstrap current below 50 kA, and reduced turbulent heat fluxes. In order to fix the plasma volume of $1500~m^3$ during optimization, the VMEC code was modified to renormalize the boundary coefficient to the desired plasma volume. The STELLOPT stellarator optimization code was modified as well to include new bootstrap current targets, a new target for the radial electric field, and the capability to hold the magnetic field on axis at a fixed value. An intermediary conceptual design plasma and final evolved fixed boundary equilibria are compared to the original modified W7-X equilibrium. The final evolved equilibrium is shown to achieve all the necessary requirements for the GIGA fusion power plant through more detailed modeling of stability, fast ion confinement, and transport.

authors.name: Samuel A. Lazerson, Ant\'onio J. Coelho, Dana Douqa, Adrian Asmund Fessler, Luisa H\"ubner, Matteo Moscheni, Eoin Hodge, Richard Kembleton, Joona Sissonen, Konsta S\"arkim\"aki, Antti Snicker, the Gauss Fusion Team

papers.title: Reformation of Supercritical Perpendicular Shock
papers.summary: Super-critical collisionless shocks are not static but evolve continuously as they reflect incoming ions upstream. The process responsible for this non-stationarity -- whether wave-like corrugation of the shock surface (rippling) or cyclic rebuilding of the shock transition (reformation) -- remains debated. We combine Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) observations of a nearly perpendicular ($\theta_{Bn}\approx89^\circ$), supercritical ($M_A\approx6$) bow shock with a high-resolution two-dimensional hybrid simulation. MMS reveals repeated ion phase-space holes and intense, localized Hall electric fields. A virtual-spacecraft analysis of the simulation reproduces these signatures and shows that they arise from a self-regulating feedback cycle: strong Hall-field ion reflection builds a reflected-ion foot, which weakens the Hall field and suppresses further reflection until the foot decays and the cycle restarts. This reformation cycle, spatially organized by the two-dimensional shock structure, can account for several principal signatures of the observed non-stationarity.

authors.name: Yuri V. Khotyaintsev, Domenico Trotta, Daniel B. Graham

papers.title: Ultrashort pulsed laser atmospheric filament properties and microwave radiation inferred from S-band guided wave interaction and self-emission
papers.summary: The electrical conductivity $\sigma$ of the plasma filament left behind by an ultrashort pulsed laser (USPL) optical pulse after it is geometrically then self-focused in air via the Kerr effect is measured by attenuation of a $3.2$ GHz TE$_{10}$ mode within an S-band waveguide through which the filament passes, taking into account the characteristic radius $R$ of the filament, as determined by fast camera visible light imaging. Models of the major air constituents' ionization rate $W_{i}$ vs. local laser intensity $I$, and of electron temperature $T$ and mean axial electron momentum $\left\langle p_{{z}}\right\rangle $ vs. peak laser intensity $I_{0}$ are then used to infer the filament's $I_{0}$, $T$, major species particle densities, current decay rate $\nu$, and current time integral $Q$ after pulse passage. $Q$ is independently measured via the filament's self-emission in the waveguide signal for comparison. The theoretical far field microwave radiation pattern for the later $Q=Q\left( z\right) $ is calculated. It compares favorably to published measurements, provided $\nu$ is reduced to the value where the total radiated power is equal to the center-of-mass electron kinetic energy imparted by the laser's magnetic Lorentz force. Results are presented for a $30$ cm long filament at a broad range of atmospheric pressures.

authors.name: Edward. L. Ruden, James. E. Wymer, Jennifer. A. Elle, Alex C. Englesbe, Andrian P. Lucero, Erin A. Thornton, Andreas Schmitt-Sody

papers.title: Exact Solution of the Direct and Inverse Quasi-stationary Dynamo Problem in the Expanding Plasma Ball
papers.summary: It is shown that differential equation of the quasi-stationary dynamo effect (i.e., generation of the electric fields and currents) in a uniformly-expanding plasma ball with strongly anisotropic conductivity possesses the unique mathematical property: namely, the spectrum of its eigenvalues is universal and independent of physical parameters of the medium. As a result, it becomes possible to introduce a special set of eigenfunctions - which we called the generalized spherical functions - that can be used to solve the dynamo problem in exactly the same way as ordinary spherical functions are used to solve the Laplace equation. The corresponding exact solutions should be especially valuable for treating the inverse dynamo problem, i.e., determination of the plasma parameters from the experimentally measured electric fields and currents.

authors.name: Yurii V. Dumin

papers.title: Demonstration of Flying-Focus-Enhanced Relativistic Thomson Scattering
papers.summary: We report the experimental demonstration of a spatiotemporally engineered "flying-focus" laser pulse for enhanced X-ray generation via relativistic Thomson scattering. By combining longitudinal chromatic aberration, angular dispersion, and group delay dispersion, we create a relativistically intense laser pulse whose focal point propagates with an independently tunable velocity vector, enabling control of both its speed and propagation angle. Precise tuning of the focal-point trajectory is used to match the motion of a near-counterpropagating ultrarelativistic electron bunch generated by a laser wakefield accelerator. This spatiotemporal velocity matching extends the interaction length while mitigating nonlinear scattering effects, resulting in an enhanced X-ray yield. Simulations indicate that this approach can increase the spectral density and brightness of Thomson-scattered X-ray beams by orders of magnitude relative to equivalent focusing without spatiotemporal control. The technique provides a new degree of freedom for high-intensity laser-matter interactions, allowing dynamic intensity structures with programmable two-dimensional motion and opening a route to enhanced laser-particle interactions and next-generation ultrabright radiation sources.

authors.name: E. Gerstmayr, C. Mariani, R. Fitzgarrald, M. VanDusen-Gross, C. Berger, Q. Chen, A. Di Piazza, M. S. Formanek, D. H. Froula, C. G. R. Geddes, A. J. Gonsalves, B. Greenwood, R. Jacob, A. Lu, A. McIlvenny, K. Nakamura, L. Obst-Huebl, J. P. Palastro, A. Picksley, K. Poder, D. Ramsey, H. G. Rinderknecht, G. Sarri, A. G. R Thomas, J. van Tilborg, M. J. V. Streeter

papers.title: Operation and performance of ProtoDUNE Dual Phase liquid argon time projection chamber
papers.summary: ProtoDUNE-DP, with a total mass of the active volume of 300 t, is the largest Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) built to operate in a Dual-Phase (DP) mode where the ionisation charge produced in the liquid bulk by charged particles traversing the detector is transferred for the readout in the gaseous phase above. Intended as a prototype of a far detector module for the DUNE neutrino oscillation experiment, ProtoDUNE-DP was operated at the CERN Neutrino Platform from 2019 to 2022. This paper describes various ProtoDUNE-DP detector components, discusses the commissioning and operation experiences, and presents the results on the detector performance from an analysis of collected cosmic ray data. Some key deliverables of the detector were achieved, including stable delivery of 300 kV to the TPC cathode, operation of the charge readout with an effective gain exceeding 5 before charging-up, stable functioning of the photon detection system with a relative time accuracy among PMTs below 16 ns. The long term operation of the charge readout system in dual-phase, however, was limited by the liquid surface and electrical instabilities. The ProtoDUNE-DP experience contributed to the final design of the DUNE Vertical Drift LArTPC.

papers.title: BART Online Open-Source Sequence Toolbox for Computational MRI
papers.summary: Purpose In advanced computational MRI techniques, acquisition and reconstruction techniques are jointly designed. For reproducibility, it is therefore important to provide an open implementation of both. At the same time, any use in a clinical environment usually requires a close integration with the MRI scanner. Ensuring long-time reproducibility and maintenance then poses additional challenges. In this work, we aim to provide a fully integrated open-source framework that can meet these demands. Methods A software framework to develop pulse sequences is added to BART, an open-source toolbox for computational MRI. In addition, a vendor-specific driver sequence is developed that can be used to run the sequence on a clinical MRI scanner enabling online adjustment of all relevant sequence parameters. Using the Pulseq format, the exact same sequence can also be reproduced offline using a widely used vendor-neutral open-source standard. Using the Pulseq format, the exact same sequence can also be reproduced offline. As proof-of-concept, quantitative MRI methods for T1 and joint water/fat R2*, B0 mapping using radial FLASH and model-based reconstruction are implemented in the proposed framework. Consistency between online and offline acquisition is validated in phantom and in vivo experiments. Results Quantitative MRI methods highlighting specific challenges of acquisition and reconstruction were successfully implemented in BART. Acquisition parameters and FOV can be adapted online on a clinical MRI system. Quantitative parameter maps from model-based reconstruction agree for online and offline regenerated Pulseq acquisitions. Conclusion This work enables reproducibility of advanced computational MRI methods within a comprehensive end-to-end open-source framework.

papers.title: On transition path times for condensed-phase non-adiabatic electron transfer reactions under a two-parabola model
papers.summary: Condensed-phase non-adiabatic electron transfer (ET) reactions play an important role in various areas of science. The characteristics of the microscopic transition processes involved in these reactions and their dynamic behavior remain much room for further understanding. In this study, we performed non-adiabatic dynamics simulations based on Zhu-Nakamura theory, combining the two-parabola model with Kramers-like Langevin dynamics. We numerically analyzed the dependence of the macroscopic reaction time and the timescale of the microscopic transition process on the diabatic coupling between the diabatic states and on the friction parameter in Langevin dynamics. Focusing on resulting two quantities, that is, the reaction rate and the transition path times (TPTs), which characterize the macroscopic population transfer and the individual transition process, respectively, we discuss how non-adiabatic transitions influence the reaction dynamics.

authors.name: Ryo Nihei, Hiroki Uratani, Hirofumi Sato

papers.title: Cavity optomechanics with a suspended resonant mirror
papers.summary: We investigate optomechanical effects in cavities consisting of a plane-plane arrangement of a broadband reflectivity mirror and an ultrathin, suspended resonant mirror possessing a high-Q internal optical resonance. We first investigate dispersive and photothermal optomechanics in such cavities on the basis of a generic analytical model as well as finite element method simulations of realistic structures. We then report on experimental optical spring measurements using a suspended silicon nitride membrane patterned with a subwavelength grating. The observed optical spring variations match those expected from the theoretical model, but with a magnitude several hundreds times larger than expected from the dispersive optomechanical coupling only, thus suggesting strong photothermal optomechanical coupling.

authors.name: Trishala Mitra, Gurprret Singh, S{\o}ren Peder Madsen, Aur\'elien Dantan

papers.title: Coupled multiscale paleoclimate reconstruction with four-dimensional variational data assimilation
papers.summary: Paleoclimate archives extend climate knowledge beyond the instrumental era, registering different seasons, variables, time averages, and memory lengths. A longstanding problem is to integrate these heterogeneous sources of information within a unified methodology. Here we present a new data-assimilation framework, Last Millennium Reanalysis 4D-Var (LMR4D-Var), which reconstructs climate trajectories from these heterogeneous datasets while balancing errors in the model, observations, and initial conditions. We compare results using LMR4D-Var to assimilate proxies from PAGES2k, Temp12k, and borehole temperature profiles without treating them as instantaneous equivalents. Instrumental validation demonstrates that LMR4D-Var achieves the highest skill in reconstructing global mean temperature among existing reconstructions. Borehole assimilation preserves skill against withheld annually resolved records, increases agreement between reconstructed 300--2000-m ocean heat content (OHC) and independent estimates, and yields a cooler reconstructed Little Ice Age ocean. Modern 130-year OHC trends in the 0--300-m and 300--2000-m layers exceed their respective reconstructed pre-1870 Common Era trend distributions. Results for Temp12k demonstrate assimilation of decadal-to-millennial records and the potential for Holocene and deeper-time applications with suitable emulators.

authors.name: Zilu Meng, Gregory J. Hakim, Julien Emile-Geay, Tanaya Gondhalekar, Eric J. Steig

papers.title: Nuclear-Electronic Orbital Subsystem Density Functional Theory
papers.summary: We present a new computational approach based on Nuclear-Electronic Orbital and Subsystem Density Functional Theory. The resulting NEO-sDFT methodology enables quantum chemical calculations of large molecular systems composed of thousands of atoms while also describing selected protons quantum mechanically. A key feature of the associated program implementation is its flexibility in assigning quantum protons to subsystems, allowing different embedding schemes to be employed within a unified framework. The accuracy of NEO-sDFT is assessed by computing energies of water clusters of growing size. Deviations from reference Nuclear-Electronic Orbital Density Functional Theory results amount to only a few meV for water dimers near the equilibrium separation and are comparable to those of conventional Subsystem Density Functional Theory for larger clusters. The favorable computational scaling of NEO-sDFT is further showcased through calculations on water clusters of increasing size, with up to 303 protons being treated quantum mechanically. Our results demonstrate that NEO-sDFT is an accurate and efficient approach for incorporating nuclear quantum effects into large-scale simulations, providing a foundation for future applications to proton transfer processes in biochemical systems.

authors.name: Denis G. Artiukhin

papers.title: Multiphysics simulation of all-optical switching and sequential magneto-optic readout in an integrated Si$_3$N$_4$/GdFeCo waveguide
papers.summary: Femtosecond pulses guided in a silicon nitride waveguide have recently switched a Co/Gd magnetic element patterned on top of it, a step towards magnetic memory built into photonic circuits. The guided mode heats such an element non-uniformly, and, to our knowledge, no calculation has yet followed the written state from this heating to an optical readout. Here we model both steps for an 8 nm GdFeCo film inserted across a Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguide. A three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain calculation gives the absorbed pump energy. This energy drives a four-temperature model and calibrated stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch dynamics, and a later probe pulse reads the recovered state. At the reference fluence, a single pump pulse reverses 86% of the film from either saturated state, and this fraction changes little over a 2.4-fold range of incident fluence. The unswitched cells lie where the absorbed fluence stays below the single-cell threshold, and a threshold rule applied to the absorption map reproduces the full calculation. When the film starts from zero magnetization, thermal noise sets the direction of each recovered local moment at random. Between the saturated and random states, the probe energy fractions change by at most 0.02. The magnetic Faraday and Kerr rotations are far more sensitive and become about 12 and 130 times smaller, respectively, in the random state than in a saturated film. The reflected signal also contains a magnetization-independent geometric background, which can be removed by subtracting a reference signal. The model therefore predicts that a guided probe can distinguish the written states through its polarization. It assumes a homogeneous film and omits heat flow and exchange between neighbouring cells.

authors.name: Muhammad Arief Mulyana, Budi Adiperdana, Ayi Bahtiar

papers.title: Physics-informed Learning for Orbital Uncertainty Propagation with Error Bounds
papers.summary: The Fokker-Planck partial differential equation (FP-PDE) governs uncertainty evolution in stochastic dynamical systems. In orbital dynamics, solving the FP-PDE is challenging because of nonlinear motion, high-dimensional states, and large space-time domains. We develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach that approximates the FP-PDE solution as a single space-time probability density, while also quantifying its worst-case approximation error. This approach is, in principle, independent of the choice of state coordinates and neural network architecture. Specifically, to enforce probability density function (PDF) properties into the neural network, we design a Physics-informed Gaussian mixture model (PINN-GMM). Then a companion error PINN learns the dynamics of the approximation error and yields time-dependent bounds that define an ambiguity set of PDFs. This ambiguity set enables rigorous computation of upper and lower bounds on event probabilities through tractable linear programs. Numerical studies on illustrative 1D examples and several 4D--6D orbital test cases demonstrate accurate uncertainty propagation, correct and informative error bounds, and improved reliability over common uncertainty-propagation baseline methods (Gaussian approximation, unscented transform, and Gaussian mixture model). Constructing the PINN-GMM requires offline training, making it costlier than the baseline approximations; once trained, however, a single forward pass returns the density at any time in sub-millisecond time $(0.16~\mathrm{ms}$ in our implementation).

authors.name: Chun-Wei Kong, Morteza Lahijanian, Jay McMahon

papers.title: Multi-Angle Beam Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy for Diffraction-Contrast-Free Magnetic Imaging
papers.summary: Recent development of the differential phase contrast (DPC) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) technique has significantly advanced materials science supported by high-sensitivity detectors and powerful data processing. Especially the 4D-STEM technique, employing a pixelated camera as a STEM detector, enables extensive information acquisition through post-processing of large datasets. However, magnetic or electric field imaging using DPC is often disturbed by diffraction contrasts intrinsic to the crystalline material. In this paper, we demonstrate elimination of the diffraction contrasts for magnetic field imaging by using angularly distributed multiple electron beams generated by a multi-hole aperture within the 4D-STEM framework. This multi-angle beam configuration suppresses irrelevant crystalline contrast and yields direct magnetic information with high sensitivity from the specimen. The resulting 4D-STEM datasets also enable additional analysis of sub-beam size magnetic domain structures, domain walls, and diffraction-related information.

authors.name: Akira Yasuhara, Zentaro Akase, Takumi Sannomiya

papers.title: Rotational covariance, continuous spectrum and non-modal growth of three-dimensional planar weak viscous shock layers
papers.summary: Three-dimensional linear stability of a weak shock layer is analyzed with exact Reynolds-number-independent base-flow and stability equations, written in shock viscous scales. For any base flow depending on the shock-normal coordinate alone, with zero transverse velocity, the eigenvalue problem is proved covariant under rotation of the transverse wavenumber vector. Its eigenvalues depend only on the magnitude of this vector, and every eigenmode decouples exactly into an in-plane acoustic-entropy branch, which carries all dilatation and thermodynamic coupling, and an out-of-plane vortical branch, governed by a single shear-diffusion equation. The continuous spectra are obtained using the Grosch-Salwen far-field companion matrices and, independently, closed-form dispersion relations. The two agree to machine precision. The vortical continuous spectrum retreats from the real axis exactly as the square of the transverse wavenumber, while the acoustic-entropy continuous spectrum is strictly damped and, numerically, its least-damped point does not increase with this wavenumber. Three-dimensional disturbances are therefore damped at least as strongly as their two-dimensional counterparts with the same in-plane wavenumber, as measured by the least-damped point of the spectrum, exactly for the vortical branch and numerically otherwise, making the reduction the exact, Reynolds-free counterpart of Squire's transformation, in which the wavenumber magnitude plays the role of the Reynolds number. Planar oblique shock stability results are obtained from normal-shock results by a Doppler shift. Non-modal growth, measured in the Euclidean norm, is far stronger in the post-shock than in the pre-shock gas. Linear optimal disturbances of the shock-layer ripple the post-shock density field without displacing the shock front.

authors.name: Vassilis Theofilis

papers.title: A stochastic modeling framework to generate 2-D rough-wall high-Reynolds-number turbulent boundary layers
papers.summary: Atmospheric surface layer flows are computationally challenging, predominantly due to surface roughness and the high Reynolds number, both of which demand exceptionally high spatial resolution in the near-surface region. We have developed a 2-D stochastic-based model for the generation and the streamwise concatenation of instantaneous, step-like velocity profiles featuring key elements of wall turbulent flows, i.e., uniform momentum zones (UMZ) and shear layers (Ehsani et al. 2024a,b), and vortices (Ehsani et al. 2026). The model is extended herein to the top of the logarithmic layer to reproduce the high-Reynolds-number, rough-wall, turbulent boundary layer measured by Saddoughi and Veeravalli(1994), without the support of a UMZ dataset, using only a handful of critical flow parameters: the Taylor microscale {\lambda}T, the boundary layer height {\delta}, the friction velocity u{\tau}, and the aerodynamic roughness length z0. The primary challenge lies in the integration of the stochastic model with the scaled distributions of the UMZ and vortex characteristics. The resulting statistical moments, energy spectra, and structure functions are compared against the experimental results. The validated code is made available in a GitHub repository.

authors.name: Roozbeh Ehsani, Michele Guala

papers.title: Predicting tipping points: The many shades of non-equilibrium and catch-22s of early-warning
papers.summary: The potential of crossing climate tipping points has reached the attention of many researchers and the general public. On the one hand, the basis for this concern is strengthening, with simulations showing abrupt transitions that may occur even for moderate greenhouse gas emission scenarios. On the other hand, our understanding of what constitutes such transitions mathematically is becoming more nuanced. This leads to challenges for the fidelity of early-warning signals (EWS), which accompany bifurcations in systems that closely track a slowly changing steady state. Different kinds of out-of-equilibrium dynamics in a rapidly changing climate, as well as chaos, blur the notion of a critical tipping threshold and imply limits in predictability. Using EWS to detect loss of local stability from data requires careful evaluation in the high-dimensional system, and may have limited predictive power in a highly multistable climate, where there is more than a single, well-known alternative state. This calls for new methods using non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and dynamical systems to efficiently probe the global stability properties of climate models and observations.

authors.name: Johannes Lohmann

papers.title: Dosimetric equivalence of deep learning prostate contours after LDR brachytherapy: pre-declared margins, patient-level acceptance thresholds and the incremental predictive value of DVH indices
papers.summary: Background and purpose: Dose Volume Histogram (DVH) indices remain the main dose-effect metrics for toxicity prediction, but they depend on how contours were made. Inter-observer variability (IOV) is unavoidable and clinically accepted, so the question for automatic segmentation addresses equivalence: do automatic contours produce DVH errors comparable to human IOV, and can these indices predict patient-reported toxicity? Materials and methods: In 429 patients treated with iodine-125 LDR-BT monotherapy, indices from expert manual delineation were compared with a deterministic and a Bayesian nnUNet on a fixed dose distribution, by two-one-sided tests against margins set from CT contouring IOV. Logistic regression gave patient-level thresholds at 90\,\% probability of equivalence. In 380 patients, eleven DHV indices were added to a clinical baseline predicting change in International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) at six horizons over 5 years, with nested cross-validation, bootstrap intervals and corrected $t$-tests. Results: All cohort-level comparisons of DVH indices were declared equivalent, with no interval consuming more than 44\,\% of its equivalence margin. Individual agreement was weaker with equivalence rates from 55.9\,\% to 89.7\,\%, depending on the DVH index and automatic segmentation model. Thresholds ranged from 0.864 to 0.958 Dice. No DVH block improved IPSS prediction at any horizon. The largest improvement declared by bootstrap intervals was 0.12 IPSS points, well below the minimal clinically important difference, across all learners. Conclusion: Automatic contours matched expert dosimetry within human IOV on average, but individual equivalence requires a volume dependent quality metric threshold definition. Our DVH indices panel provides no significant predictive power for IPSS, irrespective of segmentation source and horizon.

authors.name: Louis-Bernard St-Cyr, Anne Saint-Laurent, Jos\'e Angel Lesteiro-Tejeda, Sylviane Aubin, Marie-Claude Lavall\'ee, Luc Beaulieu, \'Eric Vigneault, Andr\'e-Guy Martin, Fran\c{c}ois-Olivier Fabi, Louis Archambault

papers.title: An energy-stable and accuracy-preserving finite volume scheme for wall-distance computations
papers.summary: The distance to the nearest wall provides a length scale in models of wall-bounded turbulence. Computing this distance accurately on highly stretched meshes is challenging because small near-wall cells restrict explicit pseudo-time steps and geometric singularities can induce spurious oscillations. To address these challenges, this paper presents a semi-implicit finite-volume scheme based on a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) for solving the pseudo-time Eikonal equation on unstructured meshes. An upwind weighted least-squares reconstruction supplies the gradients used to evaluate the cell-averaged Eikonal residuals. The artificial-viscosity term is discretized using a two-point face flux whose coefficient vanishes as the regularized residuals in both adjacent cells tend to zero. The SAV update advances the semi-discrete system in pseudo-time by evaluating the residuals and viscosity coefficients explicitly and coupling the wall-distance averages and auxiliary variables implicitly. The analysis establishes unconditional energy stability under homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, permitting a grid-independent global pseudo-time step. The system's M-matrix structure guarantees nonnegative cell averages of the physical wall distance under a separate step restriction, while residual regularization and artificial viscosity preserve the formal order of spatial accuracy. Numerical tests confirm second-order spatial convergence for the quarter-cylinder case and demonstrate robust wall-distance computation on highly stretched meshes typical of Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes simulations. The SAV formulation is independent of the reconstruction scheme, providing a basis for extensions to higher-order finite-volume methods and other nonconservative scalar equations.

authors.name: Xiaorui Xu, Qian Wang

papers.title: Imaging performance of a Single-Plane Readout Compton Camera
papers.summary: This work presents the design, development, and characterization of a compact Compton camera employing a novel single-plane readout architecture. The proposed concept simplifies conventional multilayer Compton cameras by optically coupling the scatterer and absorber into a single compact detector element using a light guide, enabling readout exclusively from one side with silicon photomultipliers. The system was validated through Monte Carlo simulations, prototype construction, and experimental characterization using standard gamma-ray sources. Detector performance for 511~keV and 662~keV photons was optimized using simulations based on the Geant4 framework, by guiding event selection strategy. Event reconstruction relied on coincidence detection consistent with Compton scattering kinematics, while image reconstruction was performed using maximum likelihood expectation maximization algorithm. The prototype comprises 64 detector elements arranged in an $8\times8$ matrix, read out by an $8\times8$ silicon photomultiplier array. Each element consists of two GAGG:Ce scintillators coupled by a 20 mm long light guide. Measured energy resolutions were $8.9\%\pm1.9\%$ and $10.8\%\pm1.6\%$ for the front and back layers, respectively. Successful gamma-ray imaging was demonstrated for Na-22 and Cs-137 sources, achieving angular resolutions of $12.4^\circ$--$14.3^\circ$ at 511~keV and $14.3^\circ$--$16.8^\circ$ at 662~keV, confirming the feasibility of the proposed single-plane architecture for compact and cost-effective gamma-ray imaging applications.

authors.name: Om Prakash Dash (University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Department of Physics, Zagreb, Croatia), Tomislav Bokuli\'c (University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Department of Physics, Zagreb, Croatia), Damir Bosnar (University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Department of Physics, Zagreb, Croatia), Mihael Makek (University of Zagreb Faculty of Science, Department of Physics, Zagreb, Croatia)

papers.title: An empirically constrained low density regime Covariant Modified Gravity: accurate rendering of galactic rotation curves and lensing resulting in present accelerated cosmological expansion
papers.summary: We present a covariant modified gravity theory calibrated to match all the galactic phenomenology usually attributed to dark matter in the low acceleration regime, including the flat rotation curves of massive tracers, and the deflection angles of photons as inferred through gravitational lensing. We first derive a fully covariant description of galactic space-times under a spherically symmetric and static approximation. This description accounts for flat rotation curves, observed gravitational lensing phenomenology and the Tully-Fisher mass scalings of the above. The resulting covariant description is then used to constrain the parameters of a minimally coupled gravitational action using power laws for both the Ricci scalar and the matter Lagrangian. The action presented hence leads to field equations whose trace, has as solutions metric coefficients which reproduce flat rotation curves and gravitational lensing observations, without including any dark matter. Using the same action for a FLRW metric results in a cosmology where a dust component behaves as effective dark energy with an equation of state $\omega=-5/6$, without the explicit inclusion of any dark energy component.

authors.name: Hernandez, X., Sergio Mendoza, Sarah\'i Silva, Edgar Gasper\'in

papers.title: Glassy dynamics of metropolitan human mobility frozen near the gravitational equilibrium
papers.summary: The doubly constrained gravity model is one of the most widely used descriptions of urban commuting flows, yet whether residential relocation can actually drive a city to this equilibrium has not been tested. We address this question by connecting urban commuting to thermal equilibrium. Using mobility data from around 30 million records across six Japanese cities over one year, we introduce the Gravity-based Origin Swapping Model (GOSM), which applies Metropolis dynamics to urban commuting by treating individuals as interacting particles. Within this framework, total commuting time defines the system energy, and temperature controls how strongly mobility responds to cost savings. Consequently, urban commuting can be analyzed through an evaluable free energy and simulated similarly to physical systems of matter, with the maximum-entropy doubly constrained gravity model serving as the stationary state. We find that the residential dynamics exhibit glassy characteristics: calibration to observed data reveals signatures of kinetically constrained models, specifically aging, hysteresis, and freezing near equilibrium. These results suggest that static OD snapshots may misestimate the effect of structural intervention: substantial improvements may require changing the urban landscape itself, through transport investment that reshapes travel times or housing development that reshapes residential capacities, rather than waiting for spontaneous relocation to reach the theoretical optimum.

authors.name: Yixuan Y. Zheng, Hideki Takayasu, Misako Takayasu

papers.title: A System-Independent Metadynamics Strategy for Reactive Training Data: Application to Gas-Phase Organic Reactions
papers.summary: General-purpose machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for organic reactions need to accurately describe both minimum-energy paths (MEPs) for evaluating reaction energetics and the broader configurational space for simulating reaction dynamics. Existing general datasets for gas-phase reactions largely rely on quasi-static optimization near MEPs, leaving off-MEP regions under-covered and model reliability in reactive molecular dynamics weakly supported; the gap is methodological, not a question of dataset size. We introduce a spatiotemporally resolved, system-independent collective variable (CV): Cartesian RMSD within randomly partitioned local domains against an expanding list of time-averaged reference geometries. The CV drives metadynamics as the exploration engine, supplemented by transition state (TS) optimization to augment coverage around TSs. Within a concurrent-learning workflow, this produces OpenRxn26, a dataset of 1.8~M DFT-labeled configurations covering neutral singlet unimolecular reactions in the H/C/N/O chemical space ($N_\mathrm{heavy} \leq 30$), containing reactive atomic environments underrepresented in community datasets. Trained on OpenRxn26, a DPA4 model (DPA4\_rxn26) is the only model in the benchmark suite to achieve transferable sub-kcal/mol energy accuracy on barrier heights, reaction energies and off-MEP reactive trajectories, relative to the training DFT reference, demonstrating the efficiency and generality of the sampling strategy. Domain MLIPs performing well on static benchmarks degrade several-fold on off-MEP reactive trajectories (e.g.\ MACE-OMol25), showing the insufficiency of MEP-anchored benchmarks for guaranteeing dynamics reliability. The sampling strategy enables efficient development of reliable general-purpose reactive MLIPs, with OpenRxn26 as a demonstration of MD-ready training data for gas-phase neutral singlet organic reactions.

authors.name: Wanrun Jiang, Jinzhe Zeng, Manyi Yang, Tong Zhu, Han Wang

papers.title: Multiphysics Simulation Framework for Continuous Ion Transport and Energetics in Atmospheric Pressure Interfaces
papers.summary: Optimizing atmospheric pressure interfaces requires balancing efficient ion transport with unwanted collision activation. The complex environment at the inlet region, including rapid pressure drops, RF/DC electric fields, ion-gas collisions, and space charge effects, makes simulation of this system challenging. In this work, we introduce MuCITE (Multiphysics simulation for Continuous Ion Transport and Energetics), which combines continuous ion injection, precomputed electric and gas flow fields, and particle-in-cell space charge updates. Furthermore, by employing improved impulsive collision theory, it can not only predict transport but also analyze the loss position of ions and the evolution of their kinetic energy, internal energy, and dissociation probability during transport. Transport predictions with ion currents and activation trends of in-source fragmentation were compared with experimental measurements using a custom-built source and a Q-Exactive HF source. The results show that the simulation predictions agree well with the experimental results and can serve as a reference before experiments. MuCITE allows users to derive ion transport, output beam characteristics, and ion energy through the configurable interface geometry and operating conditions. It supports simulation-guided design and tunable parameters to achieve predicted efficient ion transport or in source activation.

authors.name: Yihui Yan, Jozef Lengyel, Frederic Rosu, Valerie Gabelica

papers.title: Plasma-neutral collision operators for hydrogen isotopes: kinetic and gyrokinetic descriptions, comparison to fluid
papers.summary: Plasma-neutral interactions modify ion and electron velocity distributions, potentially affecting plasma instabilities. In this work we derive ionization, recombination and charge exchange operators for hydrogen-like atoms in a fully kinetic framework, revisiting often-used assumptions of linearity and Maxwellianity, common in usual fluid-based approaches. We first present a comprehensive derivation of plasma-neutral interaction terms in the kinetic and gyrokinetic frameworks. The model naturally retains non-Maxwellian features of both the plasma and neutral distribution functions. By explicitly accounting for velocity-dependent differential cross-sections, the model captures the full kinetic impact of such inelastic collisions on the complete distribution functions of ions and electrons, and not only through their first moments. We include energy losses due to excitation, multi-step ionization and radiative recombination. We show that the fluid moments of the kinetic model reduce to standard fluid source terms under the appropriate assumptions of Maxwellianity and linearity, and specifically discuss deviations from fluid predictions over a range of tokamak-relevant conditions. Substantial discrepancies are observed, even for Maxwellian distributions. For charge exchange, the kinetic model yields momentum and energy exchange rates up to twice those predicted by fluid descriptions. We furthermore show that a fluid treatment of ionization greatly overestimates the mean kinetic energy of the produced electrons. These results pave the way for realistic kinetic interactions between a kinetic or gyrokinetic turbulent plasma and neutrals, particularly in the edge and scrape-off layer.

authors.name: Matthieu Protais, Guilhem Dif-Pradalier, Yanick Sarazin, Peter Donnel, Virginie Grandgirard, Yannick Marandet, Srikanth Sureshkumar, Naren Varadarajan

papers.title: The role of distributed friction dynamics on heave-induced motion of offshore drilling systems: modelling, analysis, and simulations
papers.summary: This paper investigates the influence of friction dynamics on heave-induced disturbance propagation using a coupled hydraulic-structural drilling model formulated as a semilinear interconnection of ordinary and hyperbolic partial differential equations (ODE-PDEs), and capturing spatially distributed memory effects in the drillstring-wellbore interaction. First, local and global existence and uniqueness results are established, and sufficient conditions for boundedness and input-to-state stability are deduced via a small-gain analysis. Subsequently, extensive numerical investigations are carried out, including harmonic excitation studies, nonlinear distortion analysis, spatial amplification investigations, mechanism-isolation experiments, parameter sensitivity analysis, and broadband simulations under realistic offshore sea-state excitation. The simulation results indicate that, whilst the hydraulic response is governed primarily by wave propagation phenomena, compressibility, and boundary reflections, the structural dynamics display substantially greater sensitivity to distributed friction effects. Furthermore, drillstring-wellbore friction is shown to have a relatively limited influence on well-posedness but a potentially significant impact on stability margins. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for coupled hydraulic-structural dynamics and distributed friction mechanisms when analysing, monitoring, and controlling offshore drilling systems.

authors.name: Luigi Romano, Ole Morten Aamo

papers.title: Towards Exact Multidimensional Fluxes: A Structure-Preserving Data-Informed Framework for Riemann Solvers
papers.summary: Finite volume and discontinuous Galerkin methods evolve the discrete solution using space-time flux integrals over mesh faces, which typically depend on solutions to local Riemann problems. In the multidimensional Riemann problem setting, this integral is difficult to evaluate exactly because of complex wave interactions. In this work, we show that the exact space-time flux integral is a polynomial in the time step and face dimensions. This motivates a learning-based approach, as only the mapping from the initial states to the polynomial coefficients needs to be learned. We propose a structure-preserving, data-informed Riemann solver framework that uses a neural network trained on high-resolution simulation data to learn this mapping. Key structural properties, including consistency and mirror symmetry, are enforced by construction. Provided that the high-resolution simulations converge to the exact flux integrals and the network accurately predicts the coefficients, this framework yields near-exact flux integrals for use in numerical simulations. We demonstrate the framework using classical implosion and explosion problems for the two-dimensional Euler equations. In an unsplit MUSCL-Hancock scheme, the learned Riemann solver remains stable at a CFL number of 0.9, whereas the same scheme using the exact one-dimensional Riemann solver fails. Compared with the latter scheme at CFL=0.45, the learned scheme is slightly more accurate and requires approximately 30% less computational time.

authors.name: Yucheng Zhang, Clint Dawson

papers.title: SHAPE: a sparse Hamiltonian approach for prescribing eigenstates in metamaterials
papers.summary: Metamaterials, which store, guide and emit waves through their eigenstates, have enabled the development of devices with diverse functionalities. Yet the spatial profiles of conventional metamaterials' eigenstates are typically determined by their pre-determined structures (Hamiltonians). Here we develop SHAPE, a sparse Hamiltonian approach that enables the realization of prescribed, spectrally isolated eigenstates in physically realizable metamaterials. The resulting Hamiltonian geometries obey a boundary law, with the required nonlocality determined solely by single-contact boundary sites ($|E_{\mathrm{LR}}| = |\partial\Omega|$), independent of the state interior or lattice size. The Hamiltonians are further spectrally reshaped to open a protective gap around the target eigenstate. We validate our approach in discrete lattices and acoustic metamaterials. We provide a database of over 100 target states and a customizable design program, demonstrating the generality and extensibility of our method. Although demonstrated in acoustics, the principle can be applied to thermal, electrical-circuit and photonic metamaterials.

authors.name: Yutao Chen, Tao Xiao, Jing Li, Aodong Li, Biye Xie

papers.title: Theoretical Study of Classical Dynamics of Electron in Two-Frequency Paul Trap
papers.summary: We present a theoretical study of trapping an electron in a two-frequency Paul trap, motivated by future hybrid architecture consisting of a doubly charged calcium ion (Ca$^{2+}$) and an electron. By isolating the electron from ionic-electron interactions, we formulate the equations of motion for the electron in the time-dependent trap potentials and cast them in the Hill form. Stability and dynamics are then analysed in terms of the dimensionless q-parameters, which encode the applied voltages, drive frequencies, trap geometry, and the particle's charge-to-mass ratio. Under the combined action of the two radio-frequency fields, the trapped electron's classical motion is shown to be approximated well by a slow secular oscillation modulated by two distinct motion sidebands originating from the low- and high-frequency RF drives. The approximation method presented here enables a quick evaluation of the relation between the device-design q-parameters and the electron motion. It offers a crucial foundation for developing physical models of electron-ion interactions in electron-ion traps.

authors.name: Payman Mahmoudi (Heyrovsk\'y Institute of the CAS, Praha, Czech Republic), Michal Tarana (Heyrovsk\'y Institute of the CAS, Praha, Czech Republic), Michal Hejduk (Charles University, Praha, Czech Republic)

papers.title: Generalized Discrete Fractal Dimensions of Graph Families
papers.summary: We study generalized discrete fractal dimensions of sequences of finite connected graphs whose diameters tend to infinity. Using normalized shortest-path metrics and a general scale function, we define regularized energy dimensions for vertex probability measures and their optimized versions. We then establish a variational principle that identifies the optimized energy dimension with the supremum of ball-mass concentration dimensions. We also establish monotonicity in the moment order, stability under uniformly comparable measures, and upper bounds in terms of R\'enyi entropy growth and the upper mass dimension. Cluster estimates and explicit graph constructions show that local vertex concentration can lower the uniform energy dimension without changing the mass dimension. Finally, for uniformly Ahlfors-regular graph families, we obtain an integral criterion for energy boundedness and explicit formulas for the critical dimensions. These results clarify how global growth, local distance distributions, and the choice of scale function jointly determine discrete fractal dimensions.

authors.name: Jiantao Liu, Cheng Zeng, Yumei Xue, Qingcheng Zeng

papers.title: Nonperturbative theory of thin-vapor-layer linear optical properties: towards the optimal design of alkali-metal vapor nanocells
papers.summary: Hot alkali-metal vapors confined inside nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells are highly suitable media for miniature and cheap frequency standards, magnetometers and atomic sensors. Yet their linear optical properties at low to moderate atomic densities are not fully understood. The main reason is the complex, strongly nonlocal optical response of such systems to resonant radiation, which arises from the free motion of atoms and their collisions with the walls. To date, calculations of reflection and transmission spectra of these cells have been restricted to perturbation theory in the atomic density for the case of quenching atom-wall collisions, which has substantially limited their practical use. Here we introduce a rigorous numerical approach for computing thin-vapor-layer spectra that accurately accounts for the nonlocal optical response at arbitrary optical density and layer thickness. Our model predicts a density-dependent blue shift of the resonance that is absent in the first-order perturbative description. We show that its values are comparable to the homogeneous width of an atomic transition and, therefore, too large to be neglected in most cases. Next, inspired by recent experiments, we explore a wide range of vapor layer thicknesses and study how the reflectivity and its derivative with respect to the laser detuning depend on the layer thickness. We obtain an approximate expression for the thickness maximising the first derivative of the reflectivity that agrees closely with the rigorous numerical model and reduces to the first-order analytical result showing the optima at $l=\lambda/3+n\lambda$ and $l=2\lambda/3+n\lambda$, where $n$ is a non-negative integer. These results provide a practical design tool for nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells in various applications and a starting point for further development of the theory.

authors.name: Andrei V. Ermolaev, Tigran A. Vartanyan

papers.title: Quantum simulation of dissipative acoustic and elastic waves by Schr\"odingerization: absorbing boundaries and explicit polynomial-size circuits
papers.summary: Explicit quantum circuits for the acoustic and elastic wave equations, obtained by Hamiltonian simulation of their first-order forms, conserve energy and therefore describe closed domains: an outgoing wave reflects off the edge of the computational region or, with periodic boundaries, wraps around and re- enters from the opposite side. We open the domain with the simplest physical absorber, a graded sponge layer in which every wave field is damped at a rate that grows towards the outer edge, and implement the resulting dissipative dynamics on a quantum simulator by Schr\"odingerization, which turns a non- unitary linear evolution into a family of unitary ones by means of a single auxiliary variable. We derive the whole chain from the partial differential equation to the quantum circuit. An independent finite-difference solver confirms that damping all wave fields absorbs far better than the velocity-only damping mask. The damping step factorizes exactly into polynomially many multi-controlled phase gates. We demonstrate that gate-level simulations on up to 25 qubits agree with the classical solutions of the damped wave equations.

authors.name: Hoang Anh Nguyen, Ali Tura

papers.title: Neuromorphic Camera for Multi-Target Pointing Acquisition and Tracking in Free Space Optical Communication
papers.summary: Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking (PAT) in Free-Space Optical Communication (FSOC) applications must achieve both low jitter and a large Field of View (FoV) to support beacon acquisition and multi-target tracking. While conventional frame-based sensors provide the necessary angular coverage, their performance is limited by latency, available frame-rate, and motion blur. This work explores and demonstrates the application of an event-based vision sensor for PAT tasks in FSOC. The system employs a neuromorphic sensor that asynchronously records brightness changes (events) with microsecond-level temporal resolution. The main contribution of this paper is a comparative analysis of event-based tracking algorithms for the simultaneous acquisition and tracking of multiple optical beacons that operate directly on this asynchronous stream. The performance of these strategies is validated on an experimental dataset representing realistic operational conditions for dynamic High-Altitude Platform (HAP) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. The analysis compares key metrics, such as tracking accuracy and processing latency, under various signal-to-background conditions.

authors.name: Francesco Nardo, Nigitha Selvaraj, Klaus Schertler, Peter Kr\"otz, Ricardo Barrios, Sebastian Houben, Sebastian Randel

papers.title: When optimized geometries are not optimal: Implications for inverted singlet-triplet gap predictions
papers.summary: Pseudo-Jahn-Teller distortions can substantially alter singlet-triplet gaps, potentially reversing the predicted excited-state ordering in molecules proposed to exhibit inverted singlet-triplet (INVEST) gaps. In this study, we benchmark geometry optimization methods for 13 azaphenalenes against CCSD(T)-quality reference geometries, assessing their ability to reproduce symmetry lowering and its consequences for singlet-triplet gaps. Among the methods examined, $\omega$B97M-D4 reliably describes the distorted geometries and corresponding gaps, whereas the commonly used methods B3LYP and MP2 retain high-symmetry structures, potentially leading to false-positive INVEST assignments. We further assess $\omega$B97M-D4 geometries across 337 molecules comprising azaphenalenes, boron/nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and non-alternant hydrocarbons. Subsequent L-CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ calculations predict negative singlet-triplet gaps for 85 molecules and identify discrepancies with previously reported INVEST assignments. These findings demonstrate that the choice of geometry optimization method is crucial for reliable INVEST screening, particularly in systems susceptible to symmetry-breaking distortions.

authors.name: Atreyee Majumdar, Elamathi Selvan Samynathan, Raghunathan Ramakrishnan

papers.title: Mechanisms of Zener diode and ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction: A novel explanation in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect resulting from infrared self-emission at room-temperature
papers.summary: In textbooks, a quantum-mechanical tunneling mechanism based on electron-wavefunction is used to explain Zener diode as well as ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction. In this study, an attempt in particle description is made to explain these devices. Any object at room-temperature emits infrared (IR) photons. The process of heavy doping can cause many defects.
